On the cover of this title, I propose to give a brief synopsis of the cardinal doctrines of the Sāṃkhya philosophy, in the hope that a reading of this résumé will prepare the mind of the student for the study of the system itself.

This work is intended as a manual for students seeking to receive the profound truths in which the *Tattvakaumudī* abounds. Any corrections, suggestions for emendation, or other remarks will be most gratefully received.

To begin with, the Sāṅkhya establishes a fourfold classification of categories (tattva) based on their respective causal and productive efficiencies. This classification is as follows: (1) the productive (prakṛti), (2) the produced... [text truncated]
Evolvent and Evolved— (3) Evolved— (4) Neither Evolvent nor Evolved. This classification comprises all twenty-five principles known as the *tattvas*, with *prakṛti* or Nature being the [first].

It is productive, for the Sāṅkhyas admit no other purely productive agency. The "Productive-and-Produced" are the other principles, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth; these partake of both natures.

Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*) is productive insofar as from it the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) evolves, and it is produced insofar as it itself evolves from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The purely non-productive principle—
The *puruṣas* are the eleven sense-faculties and the five elements.
These are strictly non-productive (*aprasava*), because none of them can give rise to a substance that is essentially different from itself.

The Puruṣa (Spirit) is neither productive nor produced; indeed, it is devoid of attributes. All instruments are the effects of the three Guṇas, whereas the Spirit is by its very nature free from them.
These [principles] are thus devoid of any auxiliary factors.
Having thus classified the various principles, we now proceed to consider each principle individually.
First of all, then, we must examine the nature of the all-powerful creative agent of the Sāṅkhyas— or, more precisely,
the creative force of the universe. Thus, first of all— how is this?
What constitutes Force? It is naturally composed of the three *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and when the *pradhāna* is...
In their natural state, while remaining dormant, these three attributes are in a state of equilibrium. When the opportunity arises— that is,
when the *adṛṣṭa* of the soul acts upon the *pradhāna*— the equilibrium [is disturbed].
is disturbed, and it is this disturbance that gives rise to the various kinds of creations. Thus, the diversity of created objects is rendered quite explicable. As has already been mentioned, all...
The accessories arise from the predominance of one or another of the three *guṇas*; the predominance of *sattva* gives rise to a type of creation in which that attribute is predominant.
And so forth. Without proceeding any further, we must pause to consider the nature, the properties, and the *modus operandi* of these *guṇas*.

The three attributes— Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas— possess respectively the characteristics of happiness, unhappiness, and delusion; and their functions are characterized respectively by illumination, activity, and restraint.
enlightenment, activity, and restraint; they are so constituted that each always functions in suppression of the others, while simultaneously depending upon them. To explain this:
The threefold nature of the qualities: if *rajas* alone were the operative force, the universe would be caught in an incessant cycle of activity.
To prevent this, *prakṛti* equips herself with [the other two qualities].
The restraining agency is the form of the *tamas* quality,
which by its very nature is dull and passive. Thus, the natures of the various objects in the universe are determined in accordance with these qualities.
It is due to the predominance of one or the other of these attributes. Furthermore, if there were no illuminating agency in the form of *sattva*,
*prakṛti* would be nothing more than a mass of blind force.
acting in a haphazard manner. Thus, we have established the necessity of the three Attributes (guṇas).
Here, an objector arises and asks: "How can [this be]?"
How could attributes, which are endowed with mutually contradictory properties, cooperate to produce such a vast and marvelous structure as our universe? The answer is that it is indeed...

It is a common fact that two or more substances, though mutually contradictory, may cooperate toward a single end— for example, the wick and the oil, which, when taken separately, are each opposed to the other.
Just as two pieces of wood act toward each other like fire, yet when brought together they assist in making the fire blaze more brightly;
in the same manner,
Although the guṇas are mutually antagonistic, when combined, they act toward a single purpose, compensating for one another’s deficiencies.
The necessity of postulating three distinct forces is further supported by another reason. We observe in nature three distinct qualities—pleasure, pain, and dullness. All...

Other properties are reducible to these three heads. Furthermore, we observe that these properties are so mutually opposed that none of them could ever be the effect of a single causal agency. Thus, therefore:
We must postulate three distinct forces or constituent elements of nature, to which we may respectively attribute the three distinct properties. To these three constituents of nature...

Give the names— Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. We observe these three qualities in the universe, and since every property of an effect must be the direct result of a corresponding property in its cause, [the cause must likewise possess them].
Therefore, we immediately arrive at the conclusion that the cause of the universe— the Pradhāna— must be endowed with the three Attributes (guṇas).
Thus far regarding the activity of the Guṇas; we must now turn our attention toward Prakṛti, the most important element and the keystone of Sāṃkhya philosophy.
What, then, is this Prakṛti? Does it represent the Theistic God? Or the Buddhist "sensations"? Or does it correspond to the Vedāntic "Māyā"? To all this we reply—it is...

All these [attributes], and yet it is neither of these. It resembles the Vedāntic *māyā* insofar as it is the single root of the universe—a quality attributed to *māyā* as well, given that the universe is considered illusory. However, [it differs]...

The fact of its being the root of the universe is similar to that of the *prakṛti* of the Sāṅkhya; it is not God. Since it is said to be devoid of consciousness, it is merely insentient matter (*jaḍa*).
Possessing certain potencies due to the Guṇas; in brief,
Prakṛti is the single rootless Root of the universe (both objective and subjective), endowed with the three Guṇas and subject to evolution.
Through these, every kind of existence—save, of course, for the *puruṣa* or Spirit—is produced.
The next point we must consider is: how [does this occur]?
Do the Sāṃkhyas prove the existence, rootlessness, and eternity of this Prakṛti? Is it necessary to postulate such a rootless root that is itself unmanifested, yet manifests all objective phenomena?

subjective existence? The proofs for this are set forth in detail in all the treatises on Sāṃkhya philosophy; therefore, it would not be entirely out of place here to briefly summarize them. However...

Before we proceed with this, it is necessary to explain the Sāṃkhya doctrine of causality, upon which the entire structure of Prakṛti rests. What, then, is the cause, and how is it related [to its effect]?
As for the effect: the cause is defined as a substance in which the effect exists in a latent state. Therefore, it must be said that the effect is eternally existent—primarily in its latent form.

First, it exists in a potential state within the cause; subsequently, it manifests itself and is then commonly recognized as the effect. How can one prove that the effect has been lying latent in the cause and was not [previously non-existent]?
produced anew by a cause? First: that which is non-existent can never be made into an existent; that is to say, that which has never existed can never [be brought into being].
It has been brought into existence. What remains to be accomplished by the operation of the cause is the manifestation of the effect— that is to say,
its manifestation as the effect of that specific cause.
And we observe this kind of manifestation in the production of oil from various oil-bearing seeds, wherein it had previously lain latent.
Secondly, we always observe that the effect is invariably related to its cause in some manner or another. Now, this relationship would not be possible if the effect were a non-entity; for...
Certainly, a non-entity cannot possess any relations. If the relation between an effect and its cause were not necessary, then every effect would be possible from every cause. Since, in that case...
In that case, there would be no restrictive qualification to confine the operation of specific causes to specific effects; thus,
this would lead to an absurdity.
Thirdly, we cannot deny causal efficiency. Now, what does this efficiency consist in? It can be nothing other than the existence of the effect within the cause in a latent state.
Condition. For the distinction between seeds and sand as causes of oil lies solely in the fact that the oil subsists in the seeds and not in the sand.
Fourthly, the effect is non-different from the cause; and since the latter is an existent entity, the former must also be so. To take an example: the cloth is non-different from the threads.
Because it is not heavier than the latter,
nor is any relation other than inherence (*samavāya*) possible between the two; and such a relation can only exist between two distinct entities.
No other relation, such as conjunction and the like, is possible.
Furthermore, the cloth can never exist apart from the threads. The difference in qualities and actions cannot establish any [such relation].
There is a distinction. For although a single thread cannot perform the function of cloth, the cloth is nothing more than a collection of threads;
and we observe that what one individual cannot accomplish, [a group can].

It can be accomplished very effectively by several individuals working together; for example, a single man cannot carry a palanquin, whereas this task can be performed very well by a number of men acting in concert. Thus...
Then we see that the effect is nothing more than the cause in its developed state, and the latter, in turn, is merely the cause in its undeveloped state.
This identity of cause and effect was declared by Sir William [Hamilton].
Hamilton also says: "When we are aware of something that begins to be, we are by the necessity of our intelligence constrained to believe that it has a cause. But what does..."
What does the expression "it has a cause" signify? If we analyze our thought, we shall find that it simply means that since we cannot conceive of any new existence beginning, therefore...
All that is now seen to arise under a new appearance previously existed under a prior form; we are utterly unable to conceive in thought the possibility of its non-existence.
There is neither an increase nor a decrease in existence. On the one hand, we are unable to conceive of nothing becoming something;
on the other, we are unable to conceive of something becoming nothing.

Thus, an absolute tautology is conceived between the effect and its causes. We consider the causes to contain everything that is contained in the effect, while the effect contains nothing that is not already present in the causes.
"was not contained in the causes.
— *Lectures on Metaphysics*, XXXIX.
Having thus established the existence of the effect [in the cause],...
The Sāṅkhyas employ the fact of causality as proof for the existence of their Pradhāna; since the effect is merely the cause developed,
having lain latent within it, all existence [is thus accounted for].

It must possess its unmanifested state within its cause. That is to say, the elements reside in self-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), which resides in the intellect (buddhi). Now, if we were to continue extending this series further, we would—
One would be landed in a regressus ad infinitum. To avoid this,
we must postulate the existence of a principle that must be uncaused and which must be the final substrate of...
the undeveloped state of all other substances. Thus, we arrive at a causeless cause that is by its very nature unmanifested and the ultimate cause of everything; and to this [the Sāṅkhyas...]
Give them the names "Pradhāna," "Prakṛti," or "Avyakta. Secondly, we observe that all the categories from Buddhi downwards are finite and are the manifestations of something else.
Furthermore, there is the ultimate principle, which is Pradhāna.
Having thus established the existence of Pradhāna, we must now define its attributes as well as those of its effects.
Observe where the distinction lies.
To do so, we must first consider the properties of the manifested principles— the effects of Pradhāna.
These are caused and, as a necessary consequence of this,
are transitory, limited, mobile, manifold, dependent (upon the activity of the *pradhāna*), and composed of parts; these are their characteristics.
The distinctions wherein the Pradhāna differs from the manifested principles,
such as Buddhi and the rest, are as follows: for the Pradhāna, as has already been explained, is the uncaused root of the universe, and as such—
It must be eternal. And since the entire universe is the result of its evolution, it must be all-pervading; as a necessary consequence—

Consequently, it is immovable—that is, it cannot move in the sense of going from one place to another. Furthermore, because it is all-pervasive, it must be one. It is independent, not depending [on anything else].
[The Sāṃkhya school maintains] only the activity of its own constituent guṇas.
These are the points of difference. The points of agreement are that both the pradhāna and the manifested principles are...

First, [the two] would be the results of the various actions of the three *gaṇas*. Second, since both would be devoid of intelligence, they would necessarily lack discrimination, for discrimination is the result of intelligence.
Thirdly, both of these serve as objects of enjoyment for the Spirit. Fourthly, because they are devoid of consciousness, they can never be perceivers; they must always remain the perceived.
And thus it is common. This is a technical point requiring some explanation: every object that is observed is so [perceived], not otherwise.

They are perceived by different individuals, yet they are common objects of observation for all and are thus common in that sense. Fifthly, they are devoid of intelligence; the only principle endowed with intelligence is...
Intelligence being the Spirit. Sixthly, they are prolific, meaning they are endowed with evolving energy; the Spirits lack this.
Briefly stated, these are the points of agreement and difference.
between the Pradhāna on one hand and its effects on the other.
Now we must consider the nature of the Spirits (puruṣa) and examine what the Sāṅkhyas have to say regarding their existence, number, and [other characteristics].
properties. However, before proceeding with this, we must first examine whether it is necessary to posit a distinct principle in the form of innumerable spirits. On this point, the first reason is...
What presents itself is the fact that we have not yet obtained any principle that can supply the intelligence. Certainly, intelligence cannot belong to the buddhi, for it is material, being...
Since Prakṛti is essentially non-intelligent,
that which is absent in the cause cannot manifest in the effect; therefore, there must be a distinct principle of intelligence.
Secondly, we observe in our daily life that everything corporeal exists for the use of another, such as a bed, a chair, and so forth;
and we have previously seen that all the principles [tattvas] derived from Prakṛti [are likewise].
Downwards they are embodied. Although this may sound somewhat absurd regarding *prakṛti*, *buddhi*, and *ahaṃkāra*, we must not forget that these principles are, in appearance, immaterial.

The doctrine of the Vaiśeṣika school, founded by Kaṇāda, maintains that the entire universe is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*). These atoms are eternal, partless, and possess specific qualities such as color, taste, smell, and touch. Through the conjunction of these atoms, the various objects of the world are produced. When a certain individual is not a Brāhmaṇa, he can never be a Kaṭha (a specific class of Brāhmaṇas). Therefore, the author—when he laid down that "the reverse of that which possesses... [proceeds to state: "is not a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, by means of this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is established that the Kaṭhas are indeed Brāhmaṇas. Consequently, since the Kaṭhas are included within the category of Brāhmaṇas, the performance of the *Agnihotra* sacrifice is established for them as well. Furthermore, because the Kaṭhas are a sub-class of the Brāhmaṇas, they are entitled to perform all Vedic rites (*śrauta-karmāṇi*) as well. This is the intended meaning. As for the statement, "The Kaṭhas and Kalāpas are Brāhmaṇas," it is merely a restatement of what is already known from the aforementioned negative concomitance. It is not, however, a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the rule that "one should not study the text of another's school" (*na-anyasya śākhām adhīyīta*). Nor does this sentence serve to establish the fact that the Kaṭhas are Brāhmaṇas; for that has already been established through the previously mentioned negative concomitance. Moreover, even if one were to accept that this sentence serves as a positive injunction (*vidhi*), it would still result in the undesirable consequence of making the Veda non-eternal (*anitya*). For instance, if one were to say, "Devadatta is a Brāhmaṇa," it would follow that Devadatta was not previously a Brāhmaṇa, and thus the Veda would be subject to temporal limitation. Therefore, the sentence "The Kaṭhas and Kalāpas are Brāhmaṇas" is merely a descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the aforementioned negative concomitance. Consequently, the Kaṭhas are entitled to perform the *Agnihotra* and other such rites solely by virtue of their being Brāhmaṇas. It is not the case that they are entitled to these rites simply because they belong to the Kaṭha school. This is because the entitlement to perform the *Agnihotra* and other rites is determined by the universal class (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇahood, not by the specific sub-class of Kaṭha-hood. Thus, the conclusion is that the Kaṭhas are entitled to perform the *Agnihotra* and other rites by virtue of their status as Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, the view that the Kaṭhas are entitled to perform the *Agnihotra* and other rites solely because they are Brāhmaṇas is the correct one. This is the final position. This is because the class of Brāhmaṇahood is more extensive (*vyāpaka*) than the class of Kaṭha-hood. Since the class of Brāhmaṇahood pervades the class of Kaṭha-hood, the former is the basis for entitlement, not the latter. The commentary on the *Dvādaśadarśana* composed by the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra, the eminent scholar of Mithilā and author of the *Nilitaṇtrāparatantra-pratibhā*, together with occasional marginal notes.

By the middle son of the illustrious Tīrthanātha Śarmā, known by the name Jhō— a preeminent ascetic who was the ornament of the Mithilā region— who holds the title of *Māster Āf Arts* and serves as the Superintendent of the Royal Sarasvatī Bhavana in Darabhaṅgā; by this descendant of the Jhō lineage...
Edited by Gaṅgānātha Śarmā of Mithilā,
and published by the learned and devoted Tukārām Jāvaji, resident of Bombay.
It was printed at the printing press named *Tattvavivecaka* located in that city.
Preface, 1896. When did the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra, whose intellect was independent of all other systems of thought, compose his work?

It is not possible to determine this with absolute certainty; however, it is highly probable that this author of the *Tātparya-pariśuddhi* adorned the region of Mithilā sometime prior to the year 1000 of the Christian era. For the commentary on his *Tātparya-pariśuddhi*, namely the *Pariśuddhi*, composed by the venerable Udayanācārya, still exists today.

It is determined from the *Saptaśatī* composed by Govardhanācārya, as well as from stone inscriptions discovered in Bengal, that this Udayana lived during the time of Lakṣmaṇasena, the ruler of Bengal. As for Tārānātha Tarkavācaspati’s claim that "this [Udayana] is later than Śrīharṣa, the author of the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*," that is merely a product of his imagination; for in the *Khaṇḍanakhādya*...
The refutation of the *Kārikās* composed by Udayana, as well as the definitions stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*, has been performed many times.

Furthermore, Udayana composed a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the works of Vācaspati, and Gaṅgeśa also cited Vācaspati with authority under the designation "the Commentator" (*ṭīkākāra*). The seed of error regarding the "Logician-Vācaspati" (Tarkavācaspati) [is found in] the *Khaṇḍana*—
The work is named *Dvāra*, but it should be noted that its author is another Vācaspati—the author of the *Triṃśac-chāstra-nibandha*—who resided in the city of Sugauna in Mithilā.
It is almost certain that this great soul was a Maithila Brāhmaṇa; even today, [he is remembered] in Mithilā.

There is a city named Bhāmā (also known as Bhāmatī), and therein exists an ancient reservoir called Bhāmatī. According to ancient inscriptions, the capital of the Kirāta king Anyadeva— who ruled over Mithilā more than nineteen hundred years after the beginning of the Śaka era— was located in the region of Nepal.

It is inferred from Śeṣa and others; moreover, it is well known that the Kirātas have men as their vehicles (*naravāhana*). Consequently, the concluding statement in the *Bhāmatī*, "The composition was made by me at the glorious Nṛga," is also consistent. Furthermore, there is another reason for his being a Maithila: the author of the *Nyāyasūtra*, Gautama, was a Maithila, and the author of the *Nyāyavārttika*, the teacher Udyotakara, was a Maithila.

Udayana of Mithilā was the author of the *Vārtika-tātparya-pariśuddhi*; therefore, it cannot even enter the realm of doubt that the author of the *Tātparya* [the *Nyāya-vārtika-tātparya-ṭīkā*], who lived in another region and fell between those two, was merely a superfluous appendage (*antargaḍu*). Furthermore, Śrīdhara, who was a contemporary of Pakṣadharamiśra (living toward the end of the fifteenth century CE), [mentions] Śrīkaṇṭha—who preceded him—elsewhere in Mithilā as a master of Nyāya...

It is well known among scholars that there was not even a discussion of the *Śāstra* [Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika]. Furthermore, the Maithilas [prided themselves] on their own country's learned men with the verse: "Only Śaṅkara and Vācaspati are the equals of Laṅkara and Vācaspati; as for one who could rival Pakṣadhara, he remains unobserved anywhere."
Even the respectful mention of my kinsman Vācaspati deserves inclusion within the category of proofs for my Maithila origin.

To this effect, there is a verse inscribed on a foundation stone at ‘Simaraunagaḍhī’ in the Mithilā region: "In the Śaka year measured by the Nandas, Anusvāras, and the Moon (1401), in its month of Śrāvaṇa, during the bright fortnight, on the lunar day established by the sages (the seventh), under the Svātī nakṣatra, on Saturday, in the Karivairi lagna, [the illustrious Nā...]"
May the Lord of Nyedavaṇṭa establish this as a sacred site (vāstu).

Furthermore, although there exist various treatises on the Sāṃkhya system—such as the *Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya*, the *Sāṃkhyacandrikā*, and the *Sāṃkhyasāra*—which are currently being read and taught, it is the *Tattvakaumudī* alone that is held in high esteem by the most distinguished scholars; thus [it is summarized].

It is indeed worthy of praise. For, by virtue of the profundity of its words and meanings, the richness of its subject matter, and its aesthetic charm, this letter of the Lord of Speech (Bhartṛhari) stands at the very pinnacle of all treatises on every branch of learning. Consequently, although this jewel of a work has been printed many times, the noble-minded have not been fully satisfied; thus, they are eager to print it once again—[the edition] from Tukārām... located in the city of Mumbai.

The venerable grandfather entrusted the burden of editing and other tasks directly to the esteemed Bābū Śrī Govindadāsa, the foremost among the scholars residing in Kāśī; and by me, the manuscripts—both handwritten and printed—have been collected.
However, due to the extensive study, teaching, and dissemination of this work, there are no significant variant readings worthy of detailed examination.
