It has also been stated that it is not something one does not wish to abandon: "The affliction by the threefold suffering... [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī]...
"Father! [he said]. "The triad of sufferings is the *duḥkhatraya*.
It consists indeed of the internal (*ādhyātmika*), the external (*ādhibhautika*), and the celestial (*ādhidaivika*).
Among these, the internal is of two kinds: bodily and mental."

Bodily suffering is caused by the imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman); mental suffering is rooted in desire, anger, greed, delusion, fear, envy, despondency, and the failure to perceive the true nature of sense objects. All of this is called "internal" (ādhyātmika) suffering because it is to be remedied by internal means. Suffering to be remedied by external means is twofold: that which pertains to other beings (ādhibhautika) and that which pertains to divine or celestial forces (ādhidaivika).

Among these, the *ādhibhautika* [suffering] is caused by humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings; the *ādhidaivika*, however, is based on possession by *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *vināyakas*, *grahas*, and so forth. This suffering, which is to be personally experienced by each individual, is a specific transformation of *rajas* (the quality of passion) and cannot be denied. By means of this triad of sufferings, within—
"Affliction" (*abhighāta*) is the connection of the power of volition with that which exists within the body by virtue of being experienced as disagreeable.

By this much, it has been stated that being experienced as disagreeable is the cause for the desire to abandon [it]. Although suffering is not actually suppressed, it will be demonstrated later that its overcoming is nevertheless possible. Therefore—
"Appropriate [is the phrase] 'the cause for its removal. "Its remover" (*tadapaghātaka*) means the remover of those three types of suffering.

There is a reference (*parāmarśa*) by the word "that" (*tat*) to the subordinate member as well, because it is proximate in the mind. And the intention is that the cause which removes [suffering] is that which is propounded by the treatise, and nothing else.

Here an objection is raised: “If [the purpose is] seen, then that [treatise] is useless. This is the meaning: Let it be granted, then, that there is a visible means that is easy to perform; let the threefold suffering be what is to be abandoned; let it be possible for someone to abandon it through the existence of such a means; and let the means accessible through the treatise be capable of accomplishing that.
There would follow the consequence of the futility of the desire to know (jijñāsā).

Even so, it is not proper for discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) to have a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding this [tattvajñāna], because there exists an easily accessible means for its eradication that is already perceived; whereas the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is exceedingly difficult to achieve, being accomplished only through the arduous effort of a succession of practices over many lifetimes. And thus, worldly people—
In that regard, suffering does not first exist;
rather, there is the demonstration of the existence of the three types of suffering.
And the means of accomplishment.
There is a popular proverb: "If one should find honey on the threshold, why would he go to the mountain?
When the desired object is already accomplished, what wise man would exert further effort?"

1. Of that which is a subordinate member of a compound; 2. by the word *tat* situated within a compound. [Kārikā 2] And there exist hundreds of means for the alleviation of bodily suffering that are easy to perform, provided by the best of physicians—

It has been taught: for the remedy of mental anguish as well, the attainment of objects such as attractive women, drink, food, ointments, garments, and ornaments is an easily accomplished means. Likewise, for the remedy of suffering caused by other beings (ādhibhautika), proficiency through the study of the treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra) and dwelling in places free from danger are the remedies.

The remedy is as easy as a sixteenth of a mustard seed; likewise, even for the superhuman (ādhidevika) affliction, the employment of gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, is an easily accessible means of counteraction.
The Necessity of Inquiry into the Treatise (6): Refuting the Charge of Futility— Regarding the Enumerated Means.
There is no vision of the ultimate and final cessation of suffering.
He refutes this with the word “no. Why? “Because of its absence both absolutely and ultimately. “Absolute” (*ekānta*) refers to the certainty of the cessation of suffering;
“ultimate” (*atyanta*) refers to the non-recurrence of suffering once it has ceased. [The negation applies] to these two.

The absence [of something] in an absolute and ultimate sense is "absolute and ultimate non-existence" (*ekāntātyantato 'bhāvaḥ*). The suffix *tasi* is used here in place of the genitive case ending. What is meant is this:
even when one employs means such as the practice of the science of ethics, mantras, and so forth, for one who desires the elixir of immortality and the like, [the result does not occur].
Because one does not observe the cessation of each respective internal and other forms of suffering, there is uncertainty (*anaikāntikatva*);

and because even that which has ceased is seen to arise again, there is non-finality (*anātyantikatva*). Thus, although it is easy [to attempt], no observed means for the certain and final cessation of suffering exists; this is the meaning of the statement that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not purposeless.

Although suffering (*duḥkha*) is inauspicious, nevertheless, because it is renowned as that which destroys suffering, its removal is indeed auspicious; thus, it is appropriate for it to serve as an auspicious invocation at the beginning of a treatise.
The glorification of that [is as follows]: || 1 ||

It might be argued: "Let there be no visible means; however, the Vedic collection of rituals, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others—which lasts for a year and ends only with death—[removes] the threefold suffering in an absolute and ultimate manner."
[The Vedic injunction] will lead a person to the state of a goat or a pig; furthermore, there is the scriptural text, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice.
Consequently, the inquiry into the subject matter of the scripture would again result in futility.

"And heaven"—this is the author's statement that "this" (which is about to be stated, and which has been raised as an objection) might be so. Alternatively, "or this" (spoken by the proponent of existence) "might be" (let it be), for we have accepted it; such is the speaker's expression of doubt. It is appropriate in both ways. Second—
But that which is more excellent is the equality between the Vedic means [of attaining heaven] and [the means of attaining liberation], as stated:
"That happiness which is not mixed with pain, nor followed by subsequent suffering, and which is brought about by desire— that is the state denoted by the word 'svarga' (heaven)."

[Tantravārtika] Heaven is a specific pleasure that is the opposite of suffering. By its own power, it eradicates suffering along with its very root. Nor is this [pleasure] subject to decay; for thus it is heard in scripture: "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal."

Thus [Atharvaśiras 3]. Since that [body] perishes, how could there be any possibility of immortality for it? Therefore, because the Vedic means—which serves as the remedy for the threefold affliction—is easier to perform than the knowledge of discrimination (vivekajñāna), which must be accomplished through the exertions of a succession of many births lasting for moments, watches, days and nights, months, and years, [the latter] is once again rendered useless.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The revealed [means] is like the perceptible; for it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess.
Its opposite is superior, [resulting] from the knowledge of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower. (Sūtra 2)

[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī] Regarding the phrase "even for the Vaidikas" (*vaidikānām api*): the term *anuśrava* refers to that which is heard (*anuśrūyate*) following the oral instruction of a teacher; thus, it is the Veda. What is meant by this is: "it is heard..."
Thus, it is not produced by anyone else.
In that context, "traditionally heard" (*ānuśravika*) means equal to the visible means; "attained therein" means known therein. It is traditionally heard.
Even this entire collection of ritual acts exists as equal to what is seen,
because they are not absolutely distinct from it.
And although there is the general designation "auditional" (*ānuśravika*), it should nevertheless be understood as referring specifically to the collection of ritual acts.

For discriminative knowledge is also derived from sacred revelation (ānuśravika). Thus it is heard in scripture: "O Maitreyī, the Self indeed is to be known, it is to be distinguished from primordial nature" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad), and "He does not return again, he does not return again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
In both cases— namely, the worldly and the Vedic means— it is observed that they lack the capacity to counteract the three types of suffering,
and are characterized by impurity, exhaustion, and superiority [over other methods].
The state of being joined with that is equal.
He states the reason for this proposition: "For it is associated with impurity, destruction, and excess.
"Impurity" refers to the fact that sacrifices such as those to Soma have as their means the slaughter of animals, seeds, and so forth.

As the venerable teacher Pañcaśikha said: "A slight intermixture [of vice] is remediable and can be endured. "Intermixture of essential nature" refers to the primary *apūrva* (unseen potency) arising from the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice being slightly mixed with that arising from the injury to animals.

The Vedic means are characterized by impurity and by being subject to degrees of excellence. There is a commingling [of results] with the unseen merit (*apūrva*) that serves as the cause for the attainment of the goal; this is "with a remedy" (*saparihāra*), even by means of a certain amount of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

It can be remedied by the mind; yet, if through negligence even the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is not performed, it ripens at the time of the fruition of the primary karma. Nevertheless, as long as it produces that misfortune, one dwells together with forbearance (*pratīkṣamarṣeṇa*), meaning with endurance (*sahiṣṇutayā*); thus, he is "one who dwells with forbearance" (*sapratīkṣamarṣaḥ*).
For the virtuous, who plunge into the great lake of the nectar of heaven brought about by their accumulation of merit, endure the tiny sparks of the fire of suffering produced by mere evil.

Nor is it correct to say that the general scripture, "One should not harm any living beings," is sublated by the specific scriptural injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma"— that is, to prove that [the latter] is a cause of misfortune— because there is no contradiction. Only in the case of a contradiction...

For the weak is indeed sublated by the stronger; yet there is no contradiction here, because their spheres of application are distinct. To explain: by the prohibition "one shall not kill," it is made known that killing is a cause of harm (*anartha*), but its status as a means to a ritual purpose (*kratvarthatva*) is not thereby negated, as in the injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma."

By this statement, the fact that animal sacrifice serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*) is expressed, not the absence of its being a cause of evil; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between its being a cause of evil and its being a benefactor to the ritual. For while violence will bring about a fault in the person, it will nevertheless benefit the ritual.

Furthermore, the properties of decay and excellence, though residing in the fruit, are metaphorically attributed to the means. Moreover, the perishability of heaven and other such results is inferred from the fact that they are effects, provided that their cause exists— namely, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other Vedic rituals.

The demonstration of superiority: while [the Agnihotra] is the means for heaven alone, the Vājapeya and other sacrifices lead to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); thus, there is a state of being endowed with excellence. For the excellence of another's prosperity causes pain to a person of inferior prosperity.
Furthermore, the statement "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" refers to immortality as long-lasting duration.

(13) He indicates that the scriptural mention of immortality (*amṛtatva*) is an indirect indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). As they say: "The avoidance of the objection [that immortality is impossible] is by means of its being an indicator through long duration."
Because of being [the cause].
“The state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality.”
And for this very reason, the Śruti says: "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone did they attain immortality; [they reached] the highest heaven.
[Otherwise], there would be the fault of two injunctions. Knowledge of the subject matter of the scripture is what leads to the highest good (*śreyas*).
[Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.20] "That which is placed in the cave shines forth, which the ascetics enter";
likewise [Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 10.5]: "Through ritual action the seers settled upon death, being possessed of progeny and seeking wealth."
And likewise: "So too other seers who were wise attained immortality beyond all actions."
Intending all this, he says: "That which is the opposite of that is better, through the discernment of the manifest and the unmanifest" (1.4).

[This refers to] the worldly and Vedic [means]. Therefore, compared to those means for the removal of suffering derived from tradition (*ānuśravika*)—such as the drinking of *soma* and the like—which are impure, non-eternal, and surpassable, [the means consisting of] knowledge of the subject matter of the scripture [is superior].
Demonstration of the superiority of *nasya*.

It is the opposite of [the fruit of ritual action] because it is pure, being free from the admixture of violence (*hiṃsā*) and so forth; its fruit is eternal and unsurpassed, since scripture declares that there is no repeated return [to saṃsāra]. Nor is it logical that the fruit should be impermanent merely because it is an effect (*kārya*), for while an effect that is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is indeed thus [impermanent], this is not the case for the effect that consists in the destruction of suffering (*duḥkhapradhvaṃsana*).

Because it is the opposite of that. Nor is there the production of another suffering, since when the cause ceases to operate, the effect does not arise, and because the operation of the cause continues until the birth of discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*). This will be demonstrated later on.

As for the literal meaning of the words: "Therefore, [the means] which is the opposite of that" refers to the cause that removes suffering; for this very reason, it is superior. The literal meaning of the phrase "which is the opposite of that" is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) consisting of the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. It is the cause that removes suffering; therefore, it is more excellent than the traditional (*ānuśravika*) means.
For the Śrāvaka is praiseworthy because his practice is prescribed by the Vedas and because it brings about the removal of suffering to some extent;

likewise, the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa is also praiseworthy. Between these two praiseworthy states, the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa is superior.

From what, then, does its origin arise? To this he says: "From the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower. The manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower are the "manifest-unmanifest-Knower" (vyaktāvyaktajña), [which constitute] the subject matter of the treatise. (16)

The knowledge of those [principles] through discernment is the knowledge of the reality that destroys suffering; this is the demonstration of the attainment of the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*). First comes the knowledge of the Manifest (*vyakta*), followed by the knowledge of its cause, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
And through the fact that these two exist for the sake of another, the Supreme Self (*ātman*) is known as the "Other. Thus, they are enumerated according to the sequence of knowledge.
This is what is meant: having heard the distinctions between the Manifest and the rest from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*...
4. Because the manifest and the unmanifest are:

1) impermanent; 2) of the nature of non-existence [in themselves]; and 3) [as stated] in the verse, because they exist for the sake of another. The manifest and the unmanifest are insentient and function for the purpose of some sentient being, and that sentient being is the Self (*ātman*), according to this sequence [of arguments]. (Kā. 3)
A summary of the treatise:

"Having established [the truth] through scripture and reasoning, it arises from a cognition consisting of meditative cultivation (bhāvanāmaya), which has been practiced for a long time, with devotion, continuity, and respect. And so he will say:
"Thus, from the practice of reality, there arises the complete, non-erroneous, and pure knowledge: 'I am not, nothing is mine, I do not exist. (Kārikā 64) ||2||
(17) Summary of the Meaning of the Treatise:
Nature, that which is both nature and transformation, that which is transformation only, and that which is neither.
In succession.

Thus, having established the commencement of the treatise as being for the sake of a purpose required by those who possess discernment, he now undertakes the treatise and briefly declares its subject matter in order to capture the attention of his audience:
Root nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), are both nature and evolution;
the group of sixteen is only evolution; and the Spirit (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolution. (3)

Regarding the term "root": in brief, there are four categories of the subject matter of this treatise. Some things are only primordial nature (*prakṛti*), some are only transformation (*vikṛti*), some are both primordial nature and transformation, and some are neither.
Among these, it has been stated what the primordial nature is: "The root-nature is not a transformation. It is so called because it brings forth (*prakaroti*).
(18) Exposition of Nature (*prakṛti*). Nature is the *pradhāna*, the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
it is non-modification, meaning it is nature alone. Why is this so? It is said: "It is the root.
Being both the root and nature, it is called the Root-Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). It is the root of the entire aggregate of effects, but it is not itself an effect.
There would have to be another root, because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress; and the point is that there is no means of valid cognition for such an infinite regress.
The narration.

Furthermore, which are these principles that are both evolvents and evolutes, and how many are there? To this it is said: "The seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolutes. They are called "evolvents and evolutes" (*prakṛtivikṛti*) because they are both *prakṛtis* (evolvents) and *vikṛtis* (evolutes). There are seven such. Thus:

Indeed, the principle of Mahat is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) and the transformation (*vikṛti*) of the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). Likewise, the principle of ego-consciousness is the material cause of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the sense organs, and the transformation of Mahat. Similarly, the five subtle element principles are the material causes of the gross elements such as ether and so forth, and the transformations of ego-consciousness. [This concludes] the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī] Now, as to what constitutes the transformation (*vikṛti*) and how many there are, it has been stated: "The group of sixteen, however, is the transformation" (SK 20). This is the exposition of the transformations.

Thus: a group limited by the number sixteen is called "the sixteenfold" (*ṣoḍaśaka*). The word "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis and is displaced in its syntactic order; [it means that] the group consisting of the five great elements and the eleven organs is indeed a modification (*vikāra*), not a primal nature (*prakṛti*).

Although cows, jars, trees, and so forth are modifications (*vikāra*) of earth and the other elements, and likewise curds, sprouts, and so forth are modifications of their respective specific modifications such as milk and seeds, nevertheless, cows and the like, or seeds and the like, do not constitute a different principle (*tattvāntara*) from earth and the others. Furthermore, what is intended here by "being a material cause" (*prakṛtitva*) is the state of being the source of a distinct principle. Thus it stands.
There is no fault; since all things such as cows, jars, and so forth share the common properties of grossness and perceptibility by the senses, they do not constitute a separate ontological category.

He states that which is of neither form: "The *puruṣa* is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*). This is the explanation of that which is of neither form. All of this will be demonstrated later. || 3 ||

In order to establish this matter as authoritative, the intended varieties of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be defined. Furthermore, it is not possible to formulate the specific definitions of the types of valid cognition without first providing a general definition of valid cognition as such.
Therefore, he first defines the general nature of valid cognition:
The characteristic of fear.
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony are accepted as the threefold means of valid cognition, because all objects of knowledge are established through these means of valid cognition. (4)

"Valid cognition is intended [as the definition]. Herein, the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is the word denoting the object to be defined (*lakṣya-pada*). Its etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) constitutes its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). From the derivation "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate 'neneti*), it is understood that it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to valid cognition (*pramā*).

And that is a mental modification whose object is free from doubt, non-erroneous, and not already apprehended. Furthermore, the fruit is the spiritual awakening (bodha), which is the valid cognition (pramā); the means of that [awakening] is the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa). By this, there is no over-extension to doubt, error, memory, and the means of those, which are not instruments of knowledge.
(23) The etymological definition of the term *pramāṇa*.
1. The *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent cognitive awareness) of the Naiyāyikas is: "I know the jar"—this resides in the person [when there is the cognition of a jar]. [FTkau.
5] Determination of the Number of Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He refutes misconceptions regarding the number [of means of valid cognition] by stating, "threefold. The three modes constitute the number of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That which possesses these three modes of the general category of *pramāṇa* is "threefold," meaning neither less nor more. We shall establish this immediately after the specific definitions [of each].

What, then, are those three modes? To this he says: "Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony" (25)—these are the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And this refers to worldly means of valid cognition, because the treatise is intended for the instruction of the world, and it is precisely that which is under consideration here.

However, in the case of the Ṛṣis, the knowledge of the yogins who are "upward-streamers" (ūrdhva-strotas) is not intended for the instruction of the world; therefore, although it exists, it has not been described here, as they lack such a mandate.
The counting of the classes.
It might be argued: "Let it not be fewer; but why should there not be more? For opponents maintain that analogy (*upamāna*) and other such means are also valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).
(26) [Regarding] the number of valid cognitions—
Because there might be a suspicion of redundancy, he says, "Because [the truth] is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For within these very categories— perception, inference, and authoritative testimony— all means of valid cognition are subsumed.
Because it is established; that is to say, because it is included [within it]. And it has been stated that this will be demonstrated later.
Now, why does the treatise, which has set out to explain the objects of cognition (*prameya*),
define the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) both generally and specifically before describing the objects of cognition? For this reason,
the definition of the means of valid cognition is presented first.
Its necessity.
He said: "The establishment of the objects of knowledge (prameya) is indeed from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Establishment (siddhi) means comprehension (pratīti).
(28) The reason for the alteration of the sequence in the recitation of the *kārikās*.
Thus, this Āryā has been explained by disregarding the order of recitation in accordance with the sequence of meaning. || 4 ||

Now, at this juncture when the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are being set forth, since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the eldest among all means of valid cognition, and since inference (*anumāna*) and the others are dependent upon it, and because it is not contested by any proponent [of philosophy], that very [perception] is first defined: ● At this time, on the occasion of defining the specific characteristics of the means of valid cognition, because perception is the eldest among all means of valid cognition, because inference and the other [means] are dependent upon it, and because it is not disputed by any proponent [of philosophical systems], that very [perception] is first defined:

In the definition of the specific characteristics of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as follows: "Perception is the determinate apprehension (*adhyavasāya*) of each respective object; inference is declared to be of three kinds. [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī]
It is preceded by the relationship between the sign and the bearer of the sign; moreover, the scripture of the authoritative one is the word of the authoritative one.

"Perceptual determination is perception (*dṛṣṭa*). Here, "perception" (*dṛṣṭa*) is the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), while the remainder is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The purpose of a definition is to distinguish [the object] from both similar and dissimilar classes.

The meaning of the individual components [of the term *viṣaya*] is as follows: they "bind" (*viṣiṇvanti*), that is, they attach themselves to the subject (*viṣayin*); in other words, they define it by means of their own form. This is the etymological meaning of "objects" (*viṣayāḥ*)—namely, earth and so forth.

The subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as sound and the rest, as well as pleasure and the rest, are not objects for people like us; however, they are objects for yogis and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhva-strotas*). An organ (*indriya*) is so called because it functions "toward each object" (*prati-viṣayam*); its function (*vṛtti*) is contact (*sannikarṣa*). Thus, an organ is that which is in contact with its object.
This is the meaning. "Based upon that" means resting upon that [intellect]. And "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya) is the activity of the intellect, which is knowledge (*jñāna*).

When there is the functioning of the sense organs toward objects already grasped, and when the quality of *tamas* is overcome by the intellect, that surge of *sattva* is ascertainment. "Functioning" refers to knowledge.

And it is called "cognition" (miti). This, first of all, is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); the result of this, which is the favor bestowed upon the power of consciousness, is the awakening of valid cognition (pramābodha).

For the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), being composed of *prakṛti*, is insentient; thus its determinative function (*adhyavasāya*) is also insentient, like jars and other such objects. Likewise, pleasure and the rest, which are specific modifications (*pariṇāmabheda*) of the principle of intellect, are also insentient. The Spirit (*puruṣa*), however, does not [participate in] pleasure and the rest—
The state of being the body.

The conscious principle (cetana) is the Self. This [Self], being reflected by the knowledge, pleasure, and so forth residing in the principle of intellect (buddhi)—through the falling of their shadow upon it—becomes as if possessed of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth;

thus, the conscious principle is "graced" (anugṛhyate). Through the falling of the shadow of consciousness, the insentient intellect and even its determination (adhyavasāya) become, as it were, conscious.
And so he will say:
"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient body becomes as if sentient;
likewise, although the Guṇas are the agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent. [Kārikā 20]

Here, by the inclusion of the term *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment), [the definition] excludes doubt (*saṃśaya*), because doubt is characterized by instability. Furthermore, the definition of inference (*anumāna*) is established because it possesses the nature of certainty (*niścita*). "Certainty" (*niścaya*) and "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) are synonymous terms. And by the inclusion of the term "object" (*viṣaya*), [it excludes] that which has a non-existent object (*asad-viṣaya*).

This [definition] also excludes [other means of knowledge]; for by the mention of "apprehension" (pratigrahaṇa), the contact between the sense organ and its object is indicated, and thus perception, memory, and so forth are also excluded.
[The commentary on] the words included within the definition of perception [is as follows]. (32) The exclusion of those words...
The commentary.

Thus, because it excludes both similar and dissimilar classes, "the determination of each respective object" (33) is the complete definition of perception as it has been observed; the other definitions of the various schools found in other systems have neither been adorned nor refuted [here].
The white characteristic.
These [details], for fear of prolixity.

For one who asserts that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), how could a person who has not yet understood, who is doubtful, or who is mistaken come to understand? Furthermore, the ignorance, doubt, and error residing in another person [cannot be perceived by the Lokāyata].

It cannot be apprehended by direct perception through the limited vision of ordinary beings, nor by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since such means are not admitted [for this purpose]. Furthermore,
one who proceeds toward any person whatsoever while remaining unaware of, or without having resolved, ignorance, doubt, or error, would be unreliable (*anavadheya*).

Otherwise, by virtue of being mere words, they would be disregarded by discerning people like the ravings of a madman. Therefore, even against one's will, the means of inference (anumāna) must be accepted, since ignorance and other states residing in another person must be inferred from their signs— namely, either from differences in intention or from differences in speech.

In this context, since it is an effect of perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) should be defined immediately after perception. Furthermore, because the specific definition of inference is preceded by its general definition, he first defines the generality of inference: "That [inference] is preceded by the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)."
The characteristic of respect.

Thus: the *liṅga* (the sign) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*); the *liṅgin* (that which possesses the sign) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). By means of the removal of suspected or superimposed adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), the pervaded is that which is connected by essential nature (*svabhāva-pratibaddha*); that by which it is so connected is the pervader. By using the terms "sign" and "possessor of the sign," which denote the objects, he indicates the cognition (*pratyaya*) which is the subject. Smoke and so forth are the pervaded.
The cognition that fire and so forth are the pervader (vyāpaka) is the precursor; the apprehension of the logical mark (liṅga) must also be repeated.

By this, the knowledge of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā)—that "this [subject] possesses the mark"—is also shown. Thus, inference is defined in its general form as being preceded by the knowledge of the relation of pervasion (vyāpti) and the property of the subject.
(34) "It has precisely the same meaning": this is the proof for the validity of inference as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The definition of the threefold inference.
[Sāṃkhya-tattvakaumudī] Remembers the specific types of inference accepted and defined in other systems: "Threefold..."

(36) "The specific [types] of inference are now being explained. That is the general definition: inference, which was previously stated to be threefold, is specifically of three kinds—pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa.
And [the inference] based on general observation.
Because of the difference.

In that regard, inference is first of all twofold: *vīta* and *avīta*. That which proceeds by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and functions as a positive injunction in the form of *vīta* and *avīta* is *vīta*; that which proceeds by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is *avīta*. Such is the twofold nature of inference.
The avīta [reasoning] is that which negates.

Among those, the *avīta* [inference] is that which possesses a *śeṣavat* [subject]. That which remains (*śiṣyate*) or is left over (*pariśiṣyate*) is the *śeṣa*; that inferential knowledge which has precisely that as its object is *śeṣavat*. As they say: [The verse follows: "That which is known through the exclusion of others... etc.
"bhu:
when there is a negation of what is applicable, because it does not apply elsewhere, there is a cognition regarding the remainder;
this is *pariśeṣa*," [Vātsyāyana’s Nyāyabhāṣya]. And of this *avīta* [inference]...
The example of the negative inference (vyatirekin) will be stated later.

The *vīta* [inference] is twofold—as before—namely, the *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* (perceived through generality). Among these, that which has as its object a generality whose specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been perceived is the *pūrvavat* (based on what was previously known); "previously established" means it is a generality whose specific characteristic was previously perceived. Such is its twofold nature; that is to say, its object is a generality [derived from] a specific characteristic.

Because this [inference] exists for inferential cognition, it is "as before" (*pūrvavat*). For example, when fire as a specific universal (*vahnitva-sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is inferred on a mountain from smoke, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that specific universal of fire—that is, a particular fire—is observed in a kitchen. Furthermore, another type of *vīta* inference is "observed through generality" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*), which concerns a universal whose particular characteristic has not been observed.

[This refers to] inference whose object is not [directly] perceived, such as inference whose object is a sense-faculty (*indriya*). For here, the possession of an instrument (*karaṇavat*) is inferred for the cognitions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, by virtue of their being actions (*kriyātvena*).

Although the general property of being an instrument is observed in cases such as cutting, where tools like axes possess their own specific characteristics—this is the sense that "inference is first of two kinds. On this point, Rāghavānanda Tīrtha says: "I seek the consensus of the virtuous..."

As they say: "Since it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*), sound would have to reside in earth"—this being the prima facie position regarding sound—it does not have earth as its quality, because it is a specific quality remaining after the process of baking (*pākaja-viśeṣaguṇatvāt*), and because it does not coexist with its specific quality, namely odor (*gandhena saha mahāvṛttitvāt*). When this negation has been established, since sound cannot exist elsewhere than in ether—such as in the earth or a jar—it is correctly understood that sound is a quality residing in ether alone, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*)."
Thus [it is said].
—Kau. 5] The definition of verbal testimony (śabda-pramāṇa):
Although it has not been perceived [directly], nevertheless, that which is inferred as the instrument (karaṇa) in the cognition of color and so forth is of that same kind.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that cause is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that instrument is of the nature of a sense faculty (*indriya*); and if the specific characteristic of the generality of "sense-faculty-ness" (*indriyatva-sāmānya*) were a particular sense faculty, it would have been within the range of direct perception for those with limited vision, just as fire is the specific characteristic of the generality of "fire-ness" (*vahni-tva-sāmānya*). This [inference] is of the "from the previously seen" (*pūrvavat*) type.

Although it is equal to the *vīta* [type of inference] in being based on what is generally observed (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), there is a distinction here. In this context, "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) means "perception" (*darśana*);

"generally" (*sāmānyataḥ*) refers to the universal (*sāmānya*). The suffix *-tasil* is used in the sense of all case endings. Thus, the meaning is that inference based on the perception of a specific universal whose particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not perceived is *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*. And all of this is from us—
This has been explained in the *Bhāṣyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*, and thus it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.

Because the apprehension of the relationship between a word and its meaning occurs through the existence of a cognition of that relationship for one's own sake, preceded by an inference of the cognition that caused the activity of the elder who was prompted, immediately following the hearing of the word uttered by that prompting elder.
(40) The definition of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition.

Since the word (*śabda*) conveys its meaning by being preceded by inference (*anumāna*), he defines *śabda* immediately after *anumāna*: "The scripture of the authoritative person (*āptaśruti*) is indeed the statement of the authoritative person (*āptavacana*).

Here, "the statement of the authoritative person" is the mention of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), while the remainder is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). [In this compound,] "authoritative" (*āpta*) means one who has attained [truth], that is, one who is logical (*yukta*).
Up to this point: that which is both authoritative and scripture is "authoritative scripture" (*āptaśruti*). Scripture (*śruti*) is the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence produced by a sentence.

And that [knowledge] is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*). Because it is produced by the sentences of the impersonal Veda, it is free from all suspicion of defect; thus, its intrinsic validity is established. Likewise, knowledge produced by the sentences of the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, which are rooted in the Veda, is also established as valid.
Validity.

And for the primordial knower Kapila, there is the possibility of recollecting the Śruti studied during another kalpa at the beginning of the current kalpa—just as for one who has woken from sleep, there is the recollection of objects perceived on the previous day. Thus, in the dialogue between Āvaṭṭa and Jaigīṣavya, the venerable Jaigīṣavya [states]: *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)* ...the venerable Jaigīṣavya [speaks].
He spoke of his own recollection of births throughout ten great eons (*mahākalpa*) with the following textual passage beginning with: "By me, while revolving through ten great eons... and so forth.

By the inclusion of the term "authoritative" (āpta), the pseudo-scriptures of the Śākya-monks, the Nirgranthakas, the Saṃsāramocakas, and others— which are untenable— are excluded, as well as the futility of accepting other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [This concludes the examination of the Sāṃkhya-tattva.]

(43) Fallacious scriptures (*āgamābhāsa*) are excluded [from the category of valid scripture]. Their irrationality should be understood from their internal contradictions (*vigāna*), their lack of a continuous root (*vicchinnamūlatva*), and their propounding of doctrines contrary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); furthermore, it is because they have been adopted by certain base individuals, such as barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like, who are akin to cattle.

The word "tu" (but) distinguishes [verbal testimony] from inference. For the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is indeed the object of cognition (*prameya*), but it is not the property (*dharma*) of that [sentence] which would serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for it. Furthermore, a sentence, when making the meaning of the sentence known, does not depend upon the apprehension of a [prior] relationship.
There is an exclusion [of such cases] because a sentence that has never been seen before cannot be a means of knowledge for conveying the meaning of a sentence never experienced before.
Of that which was composed by the contemporary poet Diti.

Thus, when the general definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well as their specific definitions exist, those other means of valid cognition such as comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth which are accepted by opponents are included within the aforementioned definitions of the means of valid cognition.
They are included within these [means of valid cognition].

For instance, comparison (*upamāna*) consists first of the statement, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. The cognition produced by that is nothing but scripture (*āgama*). As for this word "gavaya" which [denotes] the cow—
The cognition that "this is the designator of the visible object" is also nothing but inference.

For whatever word is employed by elders in reference to a certain thing, in the absence of any other mode of application, that word is its designator—just as the word "cow" is the designator of cowness. And since the word "gavaya" is thus employed in reference to what resembles a cow, it is the designator of that very thing.
(45) The inclusion of other treatises and other means of valid cognition within those already mentioned.
(46) The inclusion of analogy within verbal testimony and inference.

1. Here, Bhāratītīrtha and others say: "How is it that by the word *tu* (but) there is an exclusion of authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana*) from inference (*anumāna*)? To this he says: 'For the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)... Now, let it be granted for the moment that the meaning of a sentence is an object of knowledge (*prameya*); even so, how does this constitute an exclusion from inference?

For sound (*śabda*) is the cause of that [knowledge], just as by the mark (*liṅga*) of smoke the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), fire, is produced; likewise, by the mark of the sentence, the meaning of the words..."

Anticipating the objection that there might be an inference [of the sentence from its meaning], he says: "But not its property" (*na tu taddharma*). This means that while smoke possesses the nature of being a property of fire and thus serves as its mark (*liṅga*), the sentence does not possess the nature of being a property of the sentence-meaning, such that the sentence could be the mark of that meaning. Now, even if there is no relationship of property and property-bearer between the sentence and the sentence-meaning—just as there is none between smoke and fire—nevertheless, just as smoke requires the apprehension of a connection with a related fire, so too...

If it is argued that, just as smoke requires the apprehension of its relation with fire to indicate it, so too a sentence requires the apprehension of its relation with its meaning to convey that meaning—thus, the dawn has broken at the very threshold of the millstone—the author replies with the words "And not... Even though Jaimini established in the *Autpattika-sūtra* that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*), a word conveys its meaning only by depending on the apprehension of that relationship through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). Furthermore, since the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*), [the sentence] conveys its own meaning...
"In the case of being a denoter (*vācakatve*), there is no dependence on the apprehension of a relation; for the cognition of a qualified object is indeed the meaning of a sentence. [Kau.
5] Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference (*anumāna*).
Since it is a denoter, that cognition is nothing but inference. As for the [cognition] of a cow associated with a gavaya that is in contact with the eye—

The cognition of that which is perceived is indeed perception. For this very reason, when a cow is being remembered, the cognition of similarity with respect to a gavaya is perception. However, the similarity is not one thing in the [cow] and another in the gavaya; for it is said that similarity in one genus existing in another genus consists in the connection with many common parts (avayavasāmānya). And the connection with common parts is a single [entity]. If that—
Since the cow is likewise perceptible, there is no distinct object of knowledge for analogy (*upamāna*) such that analogy would function as a separate means of valid cognition;
thus, analogy is not a separate means of valid cognition.

Likewise, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also not a separate means of valid cognition. For instance, when Caitra is alive, the postulation of his being outside— which has not been perceived— based on the observation of his absence from the house, is included within the scope of inference.
This is the view held by the elders (*vṛddha*). That too is indeed inference (*anumāna*).

For when that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) is absent in one place, it is present elsewhere; and when that which is non-pervasive is present in one place, it is absent elsewhere—thus, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is easily established in one's own body. And so, [the absence] of one who is alive from the house...

The perception of existence outside is nothing other than an inference based on the mark (liṅga) of perceiving existence [elsewhere]. Nor can Caitra’s absence from the house be denied by virtue of his existence somewhere, such that his absence from the house would be unestablished and thus not a reason for his being outside.
Nor is his existence denied by his absence from the house, such that his very existence would become untenable—

One should not posit the self as being outside. For instance, in the case of Caitra, does his non-existence in the house contradict mere existence, or does it contradict existence in the house? It cannot be the former, for there is no contradiction between existence anywhere at all and non-existence in the house, because their loci are different. Even the implication of a specific location like the house by means of a general location is only partial.

Rāghavānanda comments: “He raises the objection that there is a contradiction because [the two cognitions] have the same object, by taking the specific house as included within the general location. The sense of the objector is that existence (*sattva*), being generally applicable to both the interior and exterior of the house, is contradicted by non-existence in the specific location of the house. By the statement "it exists somewhere," since there is no restrictive determination regarding the specific place, even the absence from the house is sublated; for the house [is also included].
In some cases, because [the object] is included within the term itself, the core point is that there is no contradiction with the existence of Caitra in the house.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a common location," since a generality (*sāmānya*) is a common property and the cognition thereof is a cause of doubt—just as the cognition of height causes doubt between being a post and being a person—there arises a doubt in Caitra regarding both the interior and exterior of the house through the relation of being contained therein; thus, [the doubt concerns] that which is delimited by "house-ness" (*gṛhatva*).

The intention is that, because the cognition of the agent (the living person) is opposed to the cognition of absence from the house, the cognition consisting of absence from the house cannot [simultaneously] arise. However, according to the verbal [explanation]: by means of "the general place"—that is, by the cognition of the general place—there is an "implication of the specific house," meaning a connection with the specific entity that is the house;

this is "occasional," meaning it is the object of doubt; and by virtue of having a "common object," namely, being delimited by the counter-correlativity-limiting condition (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the absence from the house.
“Contradiction” (*virodha*) is the rule that when one thing exists, the other must necessarily be absent.

Regarding the phrase “by means of a pramāṇa,” the intention is that since only a certainty whose qualifier is delimited by the counter-positive-ness-delimiter (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) serves as the cause for [the cognition of] absence, doubt is not a contradictory factor; however, the literal meaning of the words is clear.
The inclusion of non-existence (*abhāva*) and possibility (*sambhava*) within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
If it is argued that there is a contradiction because they have the same object, we say no; for [the absence] determined by a means of valid cognition is the non-existence [of a person] in the house.

For it is not possible to negate a presence in the house that is merely partial and doubtful. Nor is it logical that the absence from the house, ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while negating this partial presence in the house, should also be able to negate [Caitra’s] existence altogether and thereby remove its state of being doubtful. And by the absence of Caitra delimited by the house, [the house...]
Existence (*sattva*) is rejected because it is contradictory [to the perceived absence], but mere existence (*sattvamātra*) is not, for that remains indifferent (*audāsīnya*) toward that [absence].
Therefore, it is logical that the external existence of the existent thing is inferred by means of the established mark (*liṅga*) of its absence from the house.

By this, it is shown that the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) consists in the removal of contradiction through the determination of the respective domains of two contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Thus it is refuted, because there is no contradiction between the delimited and the undelimited. Other examples of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) should likewise be subsumed under inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, it is established that presumptive testimony is not a means of knowledge distinct from inference.

Thus, non-existence (*abhāva*) is also indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*). For there is no such thing as the "non-existence of a jar" other than the specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of the bare ground (*bhūtala*), which is characterized by perception. Indeed, all entities whatsoever are subject to moment-by-moment transformation, with the exception of consciousness (*cit*).

And since that specific transformation of the power is perceptible by the senses, there is no object not already encompassed by perception for which one would have to admit another means of knowledge called "non-existence" (abhāva).

But *sambhava* (possibility) is, for example, the understanding of a *droṇa*, an *āḍhaka*, a *prastha*, and so forth, [contained] within a *khārī*. And that is indeed nothing but inference (*anumāna*).
For the state of being a *khārī* is known to be invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with a *droṇa* and so on; it thus makes known the existence of a *droṇa* and so forth within the *khārī*.
(49) The inclusion of *sambhava* within inference (*anumāna*).
And that which has no specified speaker,
being merely a succession of reports— such as "Thus indeed said the ancients"— is *aitihya* (tradition), for example: "A yakṣa dwells here in this banyan tree."
That is not a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it lacks the status of a valid cognition due to having no specified speaker.

Because it is subject to doubt; however, when there is certainty that the speaker is authoritative, it is simply scripture (*āgama*). Thus, it is established that "the means of valid cognition is threefold.
[Kośa 7] From inference, [one knows] those things beyond the senses.
This is cognition.
Thus, for the sake of establishing the objects of knowledge characterized as the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower, the means of valid cognition have been defined. In that regard:

(51) It is evident that no one at all determines the nature of the earth and other elements through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor does anyone ascertain them through inference based on prior experience (*pūrvavat*),
such as fire and so forth from the observation of smoke; therefore, a treatise intended for their exposition would have little purpose.

Thus, that which is difficult to comprehend is to be explained by this [treatise]. In that regard, he sets forth—extracting from the previously stated definitions of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—which means of valid cognition is capable of what: "But the cognition of supersensuous things arises from inference based on what is generally perceived."
Therefore, even that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is established through authoritative scripture (āptāgama). || 6 ||

Regarding the phrase "in a general manner": the word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes this from the two types of inference previously mentioned, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and that which is based on what has been previously perceived (*pūrvavat*).

From inference based on what is generally observed (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), there arises the cognition of supersensible entities such as *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*—that is, the intellect (*buddhi*) assuming the reflection of consciousness (*cit-chāyāpatti*) and its subsequent determination (*adhyavasāya*).
The meaning is "in the evening"; and this is merely an illustration, for there is also the understanding that it applies to the "residual" (śeṣavat) case as well.
It should be observed.

In all cases concerning supersensuous matters (*atīndriya*), only inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) operates. Thus, where such [inference] is absent—as in the sequence of the commencement of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, or in the case of heaven, the unseen force (*apūrva*), and deities—those things remain unestablished through observed inference; consequently, their non-existence would follow. To this, he says: "Therefore—"
Success [is achieved] through the Āgama.
And also [the word] "iti. Since the point is established by the mere phrase "tasmāt" (therefore), the term "śeṣavat" (analogous to the remainder) is also conjoined by the particle "ca" (and). || 6 ||

It might be argued: just as perception, failing to operate with respect to things such as sky-flowers, tortoise-hair, or a rabbit’s horn, leads one to understand their non-existence due to the absence of perception, so it should be with respect to the *pradhāna* and other such entities. Therefore, how can there even be a suspicion of the non-existence of the *pradhāna* and the rest? [The opponent claims] that they are established through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) and other means; to this, he says:

[The non-perception of objects occurs] due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, intervention by something else, suppression, and confusion with similar things. (7)
1. One whose feet are grey with dust, a plowman—that is to say, a person of the village.
3. The reasons for the non-perception of the primary principles and so forth. [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī]

Regarding the phrase "from too great a distance": the refutation of this—which will be stated as "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*)—is to be understood by way of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) maxim; it is not to be construed with the preceding. Just as a bird flying in the sky, though present, is not perceived by direct perception due to its excessive distance, so too [an object] is not perceived because of being too far away.

In this context as well, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) from the [sūtra] passage— "on account of being supersensuous, non-abiding, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and similarity, as well as proximity"— must be understood to carry over; just as there is an absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāva*) regarding things such as the eyes and the like.

An ointment applied to the eyes is not seen due to extreme proximity. Impairment of the sense organs refers to conditions such as blindness or deafness. "Due to the instability of the mind," as when one whose mind is afflicted by desire and the like does not perceive an object situated in bright light, even though it is in contact with the sense organ. "Due to subtlety," [an object is not perceived].

Just as one does not see atoms and the like, even with a concentrated mind, because they are too subtle for the senses; or just as one does not see the wives of a king and so forth when obstructed by walls and the like, due to "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*); or just as one does not see the circle of planets and stars during the day, because it is overwhelmed by the solar rays, due to "overpowering" (*abhibhava*).
"Due to being mixed with similar things," as one does not perceive drops of water released from a cloud when they have fallen into a reservoir.

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By it, non-manifestation (*anudbhava*) is also included, as in the case of the cessation of the non-perception of curds and so forth during the stage of milk and so forth.
Because it does not arise, one does not perceive it.
This is what is meant:

the non-existence of an object does not follow merely from the cessation of perception, for that would lead to the absurdity of [non-existence] even when there is no perception [of something]. For instance, one who has gone out from a house [does not perceive] the people in the house—

One would not determine the absence of something merely by the non-existence of its cause; however, this is not the case here. Rather, it is through the cessation of a possible perception that one determines this absence.
And since primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the self (*puruṣa*), and so forth, do not possess the fitness for perception, it is not from their mere cessation [that their absence is determined].
Therefore, it is logical for authoritative persons to have certainty regarding its non-existence. || 7 ||
What, then, is the reason for the non-perception of these [causes], such as *pradhāna* and the rest? To this he says:
"Its non-perception is due to subtlety, not due to non-existence, because it is perceived through its effects.
And that effect, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), is both similar and dissimilar to its material cause (*prakṛti*). (8)
Regarding the phrase "due to subtlety" (*saukṣmyāt*): Now, one might ask whether these [entities] are simply not perceived because they do not exist, like a seventh taste.

Just as a lion, having gone forward, looks back, so too this principle applies wherever the subsequent word is connected with words that have already occurred; such details should be seen in our *Nyāyalatikā*. [Ko. 9]
(58) When the primary cause is not perceived,
gentleness is the reason.
[The objection: Why does the effect not [arise] from the primary cause (*pradhāna*)? To this he says: "Because it does not exist. Why?
"Because that is perceived through its effects. "That" refers to...

It refers to *pradhāna*. However, he will state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the perception of the *puruṣa* in the verse: “Because it is for the sake of another, being a composite” (Kārikā 17). For when something has been determined by a more firm means of valid cognition, perception does not operate toward it; rather, it is postulated that it does not operate because of its unfitness [as an object]. But the seventh taste is not established by a means of valid cognition.
The intention is that, regarding [the object] as "sustained," it is impossible to determine the capacity of perception to function there.

What, then, is that effect from which the inference of Pradhāna [is drawn]? To this he says: "And that effect, beginning with Mahat, is of the nature of Pradhāna" (59). And how this serves as a means of cognition will be explained later.

It will be established that [the world] arises from the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, which serve as its cause; and the effect of that effect is discriminative knowledge (vivekajñāna) and the like.
Regarding the application of similarity and dissimilarity, he says: "That which is similar in nature and that which is dissimilar. These two, however, shall be analyzed further below. (8)
From an effect, only a cause is inferred. Furthermore, there are disagreements among disputants regarding this causal relationship. For instance, some say: "The existent arises from the non-existent.

Others hold that the multitude of effects is a transformation (*vivarta*) of a single existent reality and is not substantially real. Thus, there are various conflicting views among disputants concerning the connection between cause and effect.
Thus say others; but others [hold] that "the non-existent arises from the existent," while the elders [hold] that "the existent arises from the existent."

In that regard, in the first three alternatives, *pradhāna* is not established. For the world—which consists of sound and other objects, possesses the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and is characterized by the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and transformation—is the very proof for the existence of *pradhāna* as the cause. Indeed, the fact that the world is *pradhāna* makes known that its nature consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Furthermore, if that which is non-existent were to arise as existent, how could a cause that is non-existent and indefinable become something consisting of pleasure and so forth, or sound and so forth?

This is because the identity of the existent and the non-existent is logically impossible. Alternatively, if the manifold world of sound and so forth is a transformation (*vivarta*) of a single existent reality, even then it would not be the case that "the existent arises from the existent. Moreover, this non-dual reality cannot possess the nature of the manifold world.

Moreover, the perception of the non-proliferated (niṣprapañca) as having the nature of proliferation (prapañca) is nothing but an illusion. Even for those such as Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama), who maintain that an effect arises from an existent cause as something non-existent, the cause cannot be of the nature of the effect because the identity of the existent and the non-existent is untenable; thus, in their view as well, the Pradhāna is not established. Therefore, in order to establish the primary cause (*pradhāna*), he first asserts the pre-existence of the effect:
(62) The demonstration that the effect pre-exists in the cause.

Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because not everything is possible [to be produced], because the efficient cause produces only what it is capable of producing, and because the effect exists within the cause, the effect is existent [prior to its production]. (9)

Regarding the phrase "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced": the Buddhist tenet is that "the effect exists even prior to the operation of the cause. Consequently, the followers of the Nyāya school should not raise the objection of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established). This is because [the effect] does not arise from the destruction of the seed, the lump of clay, and so forth.

Even though the production of sprouts, jars, and so forth is observed immediately following [destruction], nevertheless, destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is not the cause; rather, it is the positive entity (*bhāva*) itself—the parts of the seed and so forth—that is the cause. For if the production of an entity were from non-existence (*abhāva*), then since that [non-existence] is easily available everywhere, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of all effects being produced at all times; this is stated in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*.
This has been established by us.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced. If the effect were non-existent prior to the operation of the cause, it would not [be produced].

Likewise, since non-existence is neither connected [to the effect] nor of its nature, how could a pot be non-existent? Therefore, the effect exists even prior to that [production], just as it does after the operation of the causes. (65) Refutation of the Nyāya position.

Regarding the second case, he says: "by that which is unconnected" (*asambaddhena*).
If its non-existence were admitted, an absurd consequence would follow; therefore, in both cases, the pot possesses existence—so say Bhartṛhari and others.

"And since this [effect] exists, only its manifestation remains from the cause. And the manifestation of that which exists is logical, as for example:"

Furthermore, the effect exists even prior to the operation of the cause, because of the "appropriation of the material causes" (*upādānagrahaṇāt*).
"Material causes" (*upādāna*) are the causes; their "appropriation" (*grahaṇa*) is their connection with the effect. [The phrase means] because of the effect's connection with the material causes.
(66) And because of the relationship between cause and effect, the effect exists [in the cause];
this is the second reason. (2)

Up to this point, the following is meant: a cause is the producer of an effect only when it is connected with that effect; and such a connection is not possible for an effect that is non-existent. Therefore [the reason is inconclusive].

It might be argued: why is an effect not produced by causes with which it has no connection? And in that case, even a non-existent thing would arise. To this, he says: "Because there is no production of everything" (67), [referring to] the relation between cause and effect.

In the absence of a necessary connection (*niyata-sambandha*) between the two, [the principle] "all [would arise]" applies. If that which is unconnected were produced, then because there would be no distinction in being unconnected, the entire range of effects would arise from everything. But this is not the case; therefore, it is not the unconnected that is produced by the unconnected, but rather the connected.
"It is produced by that which is connected," as the elders of the Sāṃkhya school have said.
"There is no connection with causes that are associated with existence for that which is non-existent;

And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the non-difference of cause and effect are as follows: (1) The cloth is not different from the threads, because it has the threads as its properties (*tantudharmatvāt*). In this world, whatever [has something] as its property...
That which is destroyed does not possess that property, just as a cow does not possess the property of a dog.

Furthermore, the cloth is the property of the threads; therefore, it is not a different entity [from them]. (2) Also, because of the relationship between material cause and effect, the threads and the cloth are not different entities. (3) Furthermore, threads and cloth are not distinct entities because there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment between them.
For if they were distinct entities, conjunction would be observed, as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit, or else non-attainment [would be observed], as in the case of...
Between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment; therefore, they are not distinct entities.

(4) For this reason as well, the cloth is not different from the threads, because no effect of a separate weight is perceived. In this world, whatever is distinct from something else, a separate effect of its weight is perceived from it, as in the case of a single *palika* [weight] of gold.

By this, the first point of similarity is established: the refutation of the position held by others that pleasure and the rest are qualities of the Self (*ātman*).
(1) Thus, [the first similarity] is accomplished.

“Non-discriminative”: just as the *pradhāna* is not distinguished from itself, so too the *mahat* and the other [evolutes] are non-discriminative; they are not distinguished from the *pradhāna* because they have that as their essence. This is the second [reason]. (2)

Alternatively, "acting in combination" here refers to a lack of discernment; for nothing whatsoever is sufficient for its own effect when acting alone, but rather only by combining. In that case, the production of anything does not occur from a single cause by itself.

To those, however, who say: "Consciousness itself consists of joy, sorrow, delusion, sound, and so forth; there is no object other than this [consciousness], nor is there any property belonging to such an object," he replies with the word "object" (*viṣaya*).
Its status as a commonality is indicated by the third case ending; it is the "object" that is to be grasped, meaning it exists external to consciousness.
In the fourth [case], "sāmānya" means "common," because it belongs to many. Therefore...

The meaning is that it is apprehended by persons (*puruṣa*). However, if [the object] were of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), then because cognitions are unique to each individual, [the object] would not be common [to all].
This is the view held by the Naiyāyikas and others. The Buddhists are the Vijñānavādins.
There is a difference between the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) from the *puruṣa*.

[If] those [causes] were also specific [to each individual], then it would be logical for many people to have a simultaneous recognition of a single object, such as the movement of a dancer’s creeper-like eyebrows; otherwise, that would not occur— this is the intended meaning.
(92) Insentience is the fifth [characteristic].
(5) (93) The quality of being productive.
This is not the sixth. (6) It is never separated from that which has been described as manifest. (94) The stated manifestation—
There is an extension [of the rule] to the unmanifested forms of words.
"Prasavadharmi": that which possesses the quality (*dharma*) whose nature is production (*prasava*) is called *prasavadharmi*.

[Although one should have said *prasavadharma*, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is used to express the constant connection with the quality of production. This occurs through both the transformation of its own form and the transformation of another form.
This is the meaning.
(95) The dissimilarity between the manifest and the unmanifest from the Puruṣa.
“Non-conscious”: all [entities], beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna) and intellect (buddhi), are non-conscious; however, unlike the Vaināśikas, consciousness does not belong to the intellect.
This is the meaning.
(96) And there is similarity of properties.

(97) Having defined the qualities (*guṇa*), he extends [that description] by analogy to the unmanifest (*avyakta*) with the words, "so too is the Pradhāna. Just as the manifest is, so too is the unmanifest.
This is the meaning.
He states the dissimilarity of the Spirit (puruṣa) from those two as follows: "The Spirit is the opposite of that."

It might be argued: "The Puruṣa possesses similarities with Pradhāna, such as being causeless and eternal; likewise, it possesses multiplicity, which is a similarity with the Manifested (vyakta). Therefore, how can it be said that 'the Puruṣa is the opposite of that'? To this, he says: "And thus..."
"Is it so?

The word "ca" (and) is not without purpose. Although [the self] possesses common characteristics such as being without cause and so forth, nevertheless, there is indeed the opposite [of those qualities], such as possessing the three *guṇas* and so on; this is the meaning. || 11 ||
It has been stated that [the intellect] consists of the three *guṇas*. To the question, "What are those three *guṇas*, and what is their defining characteristic?", he says:

"... [The intellect] is not grasped by another in its state of pure consciousness, because the mind of another is imperceptible; such is the intended meaning. Even this much of the reading is printed.
It is found in the manuscript, but considering that it is inconsistent, we believe that what appears in the marginal note alone has been incorporated into the main text.

Regarding its correctness, the judgment of learned scholars is the only authority. 2. In their having the form of cognition (*vijñānākāratva*). 3. The similarity (*sādharmya*) such as consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇatva*), meaning between the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*). 4. *ca* = *api* (also).
Xkau. 12] Definition of the Nature of the Guṇas:
[The guṇas] consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint.
And the qualities (guṇas) function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship. || 12 ||
The qualities (*guṇas*)— [which are for the sake of others]— will be explained in the passage beginning with "Sattva is light and illuminating" (Kārikā 13).
By means of this reference to what follows, or by the method of systematic exposition (*tantrayukti*), [the nature of] joy and the other qualities [is established].
It should be understood according to their respective order.
The lineage of Manu.

This is what is meant: joy is happiness; the quality of *sattva* consists of joy. Displeasure is pain—the meaning is that the quality of *rajas* consists of displeasure, as defined by the aforementioned characteristics. Despair is delusion; the meaning is that the quality of *tamas* consists of despair. As for those who think: "No... [the text continues].

Joy exceeds the mere absence of suffering, and likewise, suffering is not something other than the absence of joy; it is for the sake of those [who hold this view] that the term "self" (ātman) is employed. Pleasure and the like are not mutual absences, but rather positive entities (bhāva).
Because the word *ātman* denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*). Those for whom joy (*prīti*) is their essential nature (*ātman*) are "joy-natured" (*prītyātmānaḥ*).
Other cases are to be explained in the same way. Furthermore, their nature as abstract states is established by experience.

The point is that if they were essentially mutual negations, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence; consequently, since not even one of them could be established, neither would be established.
Having stated their own natures,
[he now states] the natures of the qualities, and of pleasure and pain.
And there is the exclusion of the nature of non-existence.
(100) The purpose of the qualities is, respectively, illumination, activity, and restraint.
He states the purpose:
“They have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes.
Here too, the correspondence is strictly according to the order [of the qualities]: because *rajas* is the instigator, it functions everywhere.
The light quality (*sattva*) would set itself in motion if it were not restrained by the heavy darkness (*tamas*); but since darkness restrains it, it sets itself in motion only at certain times;
thus, darkness serves the purpose of restraint.
Having stated the purpose, he describes the activity [of the guṇas]:
"And they function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship" (101).
What is the activity of the guṇas? Activity is action, and it applies to each [guṇa] individually.
Those which exist by way of mutual suppression are "those whose functions consist of mutual suppression. Among these,
there is mutual dependence and mutual expectation.

The three forms [of the constituents] arise from the mutual union of the elements; among them, one is overcome by another that has arisen from the sequence of objects. For instance, the *sattva* [is overcome by *rajas*].

Overpowering *rajas* and *tamas*, it attains its own tranquil state; likewise, overpowering *rajas* and *sattva*, it attains its terrible state; and likewise, overpowering *tamas* and *sattva*, [it attains its deluded state].
This is the description of the three *guṇas*.

"Having overcome the deluded" means "those whose functions are mutually dependent. Although this meaning does not hold by way of the relationship between container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), nevertheless, that in relation to which another performs an action is its support (*āśraya*). For instance, *sattva*, depending upon activity (*pravṛtti*) and restraint (*niyama*), assists *rajas* and *tamas* through illumination (*prakāśa*); *rajas* [assists] illumination...

"Depending on the activity of one, there is the restriction of the other two. This means that depending on the activity of darkness (*tamas*), there is the restriction of the other two, light (*prakāśa*) and activity (*pravṛtti*).
"They function by mutually generating one another": each one generates the others in dependence upon them.
