And generation is transformation (*pariṇāma*), which for the *guṇas* is of a homogeneous nature. For this very reason, they do not possess the quality of having a cause (*hetumattva*), because their essence—
Because an intermediate cause is impossible; nor is there impermanence, because there is no dissolution into another reality (*tattvāntara*).

"Mutually functioning as pairs" means they are mutual companions, that is to say, they function through inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction. And there is a scriptural authority (*āgama*) on this point:
All are mutual companions; all go everywhere.
Rajas has sattva as its companion, and sattva has rajas as its companion.
In the pair of tamas as well, both sattva and rajas are present;
in the pair of both sattva and rajas, tamas is said to be the mate.
"Neither their beginning, nor their conjunction, nor their separation can be perceived"— thus [it is stated] in the Devībhāgavata, 3.18.12.
(102) An exposition of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and their respective individual natures.
[ Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī (103) ] The nature of the quality of *sattva* is lightness (*lāghava*) and illumination (*prakāśa*).
The state of being that which is to be produced.
It has been stated that [the qualities] have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes;
to the question of what these are like and from where they arise, he says: Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile.
The obstruction of the Guru is indeed darkness; its function, however, is like that of a lamp, according to the actual purpose. || 13 ||

Regarding the term "sattva": the teachers of Sāṃkhya maintain that *sattva* alone is light (*laghu*) and illuminating (*prakāśaka*). In this context, the quality (*dharma*) that causes the emergence of effects is lightness (*lāghava*), which is the opposite of heaviness (*gaurava*);
it is from this very lightness that the upward flaming of fire occurs. What is this lightness?

Lightness is the cause for the upward and transverse movement of the mind, just as it is for wind. Likewise, lightness is the cause for the agility of the functions of the organs; for if there were heaviness, they would be sluggish. Thus, the luminous nature of *sattva* has been stated.
[Kārikā 13] Now, the distinct natures of the *guṇas* and their necessity are described.

Sattva and tamas, being themselves inactive, sink with respect to the engagement in their own effects; they are supported by the quality of rajas. Being raised up from that state of sinking, they are made to exert effort and enthusiasm toward their own effects—this is their nature as "supporters. Thus it has been said: "Rajas is the supporter."
Thus [it is asked]: why? To this it is said: "fickle" (cala). This refers to the state of being fickle (calatva).
Thus, by this, it is shown that the purpose of rajas is activity.

Rajas, by its nature of motion, would cause the three qualities to vibrate everywhere; however, by the heavy and obscuring quality of tamas—which acts as an obstacle to activity in various instances—a state of being is impelled only in certain directions. Because it causes heaviness and obstruction, and because it turns [the mind] away from this and that, tamas is said to be the regulator (niyāmaka).
"Guru and *varaṇaka* alone are *tamas*. The particle *eva* (alone) is connected with each term in a different order: *sattva* alone, *rajas* alone, and *tamas* alone.
The state of being a category.

Now, one might object: "Since these qualities are by nature mutually antagonistic, it is more logical that they destroy one another like Sunda and Upasunda; how much less could there be a single purposeful activity for these qualities even when they are directed toward a single effect? To this, he says: "And their functioning is for the sake of the purpose, like a lamp."
Coexistence [is established] through proximity.

This is indeed observed: for example, while oil and fire are mutually opposed, when combined, they together perform the function characterized by the manifestation of form; likewise, wind, bile, and phlegm, though mutually opposed, produce the effect characterized by the maintenance of the body; so too are *sattva* and *rajas*.

Even the *tamas* factors, though mutually opposed, will follow along and perform their respective functions. The phrase "for the sake of the purpose" (*arthataḥ*) means "for the sake of the human goal" (*puruṣārthataḥ*), as he will state later:
"The human goal alone is the cause; the instrument is not set in motion by anything else. [Kārikā 31]

And here, pleasure, pain, and delusion— which are mutually contradictory— postulate causes that correspond to themselves and consist of nothing other than pleasure, pain, and delusion. Because these [causes] are mutually contradictory, [delusion...]

Due to their specific forms as signs (*nimitta*), these qualities (*guṇa*) possess diversity through their mutual relationship of being the suppressed and the suppressor. The necessity of this triad is as follows: for example, a single woman who is endowed with beauty, youth, noble lineage, and virtuous conduct—[is yet perceived differently by various individuals].

1. "Far indeed" means that there is no question at all of those who destroy one another performing a single action; this is the sense. 2. [The qualities] consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. 32.
These three qualities (*guṇatraya*) are the means for proving non-discrimination (*avivekitva*).

She causes pleasure to her husband; for what reason? Because, with respect to her husband, there arises in him a state of pleasure toward her. That same woman causes pain to her co-wives; for what reason? Because, with respect to them, there arises in them... [a state of pain toward her].

Because it arises in the form of suffering. Thus, not finding another person, she deludes that very person; for what purpose? Because she arises in the form of delusion with respect to him. By this woman, all states of being are explained. In that regard, that which is the cause of pleasure is *sattva*, whose nature is pleasure; that which is the cause of suffering—

That which consists of suffering is *rajas*; that which is the cause of delusion consists of delusion and is *tamas*. However, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous emergence of pleasure, illumination, and lightness within a single [state], because they are observed together. Therefore, [the three qualities] do not [exclude one another] through their respective functions of pleasure, illumination, and lightness, which—unlike pleasure, pain, and delusion—are not mutually contradictory.

The distinctions of the marks are inferred: thus by their supporting suffering and impelling [action], and thus by their heaviness, obscuring, and deluding—thereby the existence of the three qualities (traiguṇya) is established. || 13 ||
It might be argued: "Let non-discrimination (*avivekitva*) and the other qualities be established by experience in the case of earth and the rest, which are being experienced;
however, existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities do not enter the path of experience."

[Objection: Since the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are non-discriminative (*avivekin*), how could those [objects] possess non-discrimination, objectivity, insentience, and the impossibility of the qualities such as pleasure (*sukha*)? Furthermore, how could they possess the nature of being productive (*prasavadharmitva*)? To this, he says: "In the case of objects... (*viṣayeṣu*).
The proof of the non-discriminative nature of the Unmanifest and so forth follows from its being composed of the three *guṇas*, because the opposite of that [non-discrimination] does not exist.
Furthermore, since the effect has the same nature as the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest is also established.
Regarding the phrase "of non-discrimination and so forth": "non-discrimination" (*avivekitva*) means that which is non-discriminative (*aviveki*).
For example, in the rule *yaikayordvivacanaikavacane* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.22), the term *dvitvaikatvayoḥ* ("of duality and singularity") is used; otherwise, it would have been *yekeṣu*.
But from what is the proof of [the properties] such as non-discrimination obtained? To this he says:
"Because of the presence of the three *guṇas*. Whatever consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, that possesses non-discrimination and the rest.
(109) This is the refutation thereof.
The positive and negative concomitances are the means for establishing the discriminative discernment from the three guṇas.

11. Anticipating the objection—“Why are distinct causes not stated for pleasure, pain, and delusion, just as there are for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*?”—he says: “Pleasure,” etc. (Kārikā 12). Just as pleasure, pain, and delusion, being mutually contradictory, lead one to postulate distinct causes in the form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it is not so with pleasure, illumination, lightness, and the rest, since these exist as functions of each individual quality (*guṇa*).

The sense is that there is no contradiction anywhere by which one would have to postulate distinct causes; for even in the case of things that are not contradictory, if one were to postulate distinct causes, there would be an infinite regress.
The means of proving the unmanifest [are as follows].

Since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—namely, that "this which is being experienced is manifest"—is evident due to its clarity, it has not been stated. He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Because of the absence of its opposite. In the case of the Spirit (*puruṣa*), which is the opposite of non-discriminative (*aviveki*) and so forth, the threefold...

Because of the absence of [positive] concomitance (*anvaya*). Alternatively, having made both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) the subject (*pakṣa*), it should be stated that the reason is indeed *avīta* due to the excellence of its quality consisting in the absence of positive concomitance.

It might be argued: "If the unmanifest (avyakta) were established, then its properties such as non-discrimination (avivekitva) would be established; however, the unmanifest itself is not yet established. Therefore, how can the establishment of non-discrimination and the other properties be proven? To this, he says: "Consisting of the qualities of the cause..."
"Because of its being an effect. This is the intended meaning: for an effect is observed to consist of the qualities of its cause;
this is the proof for the Unmanifest.

Just as cloth and the like consist of qualities such as the threads [that compose them], so too the effect characterized by the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest— which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion— must possess the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion residing in its own cause. And thus, that cause...
Thus, the unmanifest Pradhāna, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is established. || 14 ||
It might be argued: “The followers of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and Akṣicaraṇa (Gautama) maintain that ‘the manifest is produced from the manifest.
For atoms are manifest; by means of them, through the sequence of dyads and so forth, the manifest effect characterized as earth and the other elements is commenced. In earth and the rest...”
Furthermore, the production of form and other qualities occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the cause; therefore,
since a manifest [effect] and its qualities arise from a manifest [cause], there is no need for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—
[it arises] from the manifest itself.
The doubt that the postulation of manifest causes is redundant because all causal relations are already established [by the unmanifest cause].
To the objection that [the cause] is not perceived through such care, he says:

"Because of the finite measure of differentiated objects, because of their homogeneity, because of the activity of the effect, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe. (15)

Regarding the phrase "of the differences": there exists the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the root cause—the cause of the causes—of the differences, that is, the specific manifestations such as Mahat and the rest, as well as the elements (*bhūta*). Why is this so?
From the distinction between cause and effect, and from the non-distinction of the manifold universe, there are proofs for the unmanifest cause.
Among these, regarding the distinction between cause and effect—
The unmanifest is established by means of the two-fold division; thus, first [the proof]. (1)
It is established that when the cause exists, the effect exists. And so,
just as the limbs already existing within the body of a tortoise emerge and become distinct—
1. Earth and so forth;
the proofs for the unmanifest. [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī]

"This is the body of the tortoise, and these are its limbs"—thus, as they enter into it, they become unmanifest. In this way, from the cause—whether from a lump of clay or a lump of gold—the effects, such as jars or crowns, exist already and merely manifest and become differentiated. Likewise, earth and the other elements exist already within their cause, the *tanmātras*.

They emerge from it and are differentiated; yet those subtle elements (tanmātras) exist in their entirety within the ego (ahaṅkāra), the ego exists in its entirety within its cause, the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle exists in its entirety within the supreme unmanifest (paramāvyakta). This is the differentiation of the entire universe of effects—which is connected to its cause, the supreme unmanifest, both directly and through a succession of causes.

But when a lump of clay or a lump of gold enters into the state of a jar, a crown, or the like, they become unmanifest. That very form of the cause becomes unmanifest in relation to the effect which has not yet been manifested. In this way, as earth and the other elements enter into their respective subtle elements (*tanmātra*), they render those subtle elements unmanifest in relation to themselves; likewise, the subtle elements... [render] the Great Principle (*mahat*) unmanifest.
The three [subtle elements] enter into the ego (ahaṅkāra) and render the ego unmanifest; likewise, the ego, entering into the Great Principle (mahat), renders the Great Principle unmanifest;

and the Great Principle, entering its own cause, Nature (prakṛti), renders Nature unmanifest. Since there is no further entry for Nature into anything else, it remains unmanifest as the cause of all effects. This is that state of non-distinction (avibhāga).

In the *prakṛti*—that is, in the cause—there exists the unmanifest cause, by virtue of the differentiation and non-differentiation of the effect which, though already existing [in a latent state], possesses a manifold form (*vaiśvarūpya*) consisting of various aspects. [The suffix *-vyañ* is used here in its own sense. Therefore, the cause exists as unmanifest through the processes of differentiation and non-differentiation of the effect that is already present within it.

For this reason as well, the unmanifest exists; thus he says: "And because of activity from power. It is established that an effect proceeds from the power of the cause, for [an effect] does not proceed from a cause that lacks power. (113)

Power (śakti) exists in that [cause], because the effect cannot arise without a cause; and this power residing in the cause is not something other than the unmanifest state of the effect. For, according to the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), there is no means of valid cognition for a power distinct from the unmanifest state of the effect.
For this indeed is the difference between sesame seeds, which are the source of oil, and sand: that oil exists in these very seeds in a future state, but not in the sand.
It might be argued as follows: activity proceeds from potentiality (*śakti*), and the distinction and non-distinction between cause and effect belong to the Great One (*mahat*) alone.
This is because of the fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the state of universal manifestation (*vaiśvarūpyapada*), the effect exists within the cause precisely in an unmanifest form.
The sense is that it is the power of the cause;
and the second [point] is that its existence is precisely as something manifest.
—Ko. 16] The manner of the manifestation of the unmanifest. (114) [The evolution of] the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth—
Since the state of being ultimately unmanifest will be established for the entire range of effects, there is no need for an unmanifest principle beyond that;
therefore, he says:

"Because of their finite measure" (*parimāṇāt*). This is the third [reason]. Because they are measured, that is to say, because they are non-pervasive. The various manifestations such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, which are the subjects of dispute, possess an unmanifest cause (*avyakta-kāraṇa*), because they are finite in measure, like a jar and other such objects.

For jars and the like are observed to be finite and to have unmanifest causes such as clay; it has already been stated that the unmanifest state of an effect is indeed its cause, and that which is the cause of the Great Principle (mahat) is the supreme unmanifest,
because there is no evidence for postulating an unmanifest further beyond that.
Moreover, these diverse entities under dispute possess an unmanifest cause, because of their homogeneity (*samanvayāt*).
Homogeneity is the state of having a common form among distinct things. [This is seen] in the homogeneity of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
And this is the fourth [section]. (4) ||

For intellect and the other [evolutes] are perceived as being endowed with determination and so forth as their defining characteristics. And whatever things are permeated by a certain nature have that very nature as their unmanifest cause;
just as jars, crowns, and the like, which are permeated by lumps of clay or gold, have those lumps of clay or gold as their unmanifest causes.
Thus, it is established that the Unmanifest exists as the cause of the differentiated entities. || 15 ||
Having established the Unmanifest, he now describes its mode of operation:
"The Unmanifest exists as the cause; it operates through the three gunas and through their combination.
It proceeds through transformation, like water, due to the specific distinctions based on each individual guna. (16)
"It proceeds by way of the three qualities (*triguṇataḥ*). During the state of re-absorption (*pratisarga*), *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* undergo similar transformations.

This first activity (*pravṛtti*) is from the qualities (*guṇataḥ*), for its very nature is transformation; indeed, the qualities do not remain even for a moment without transforming. Ta... [text fragment]

Even during the state of dissolution (pratisarga), the quality of *sattva* proceeds by way of its nature as *sattva*, *rajas* by way of its nature as *rajas*, and *tamas* by way of its nature as *tamas*. This is what is meant by the expression "by virtue of the three qualities" (*triguṇataḥ*).
(116) Regarding the subject at hand, he states another mode of activity: "And from the collection (*samudaya*). "Collection" (*samudaya*) means arising together;
it is also [the cause] because of the absence of a fixed state (*anavasthā*) and because of falling into ruin (*pāta*).
The proof for the existence of the Puruṣa.
[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī (117) From Prakṛti...]

The wind [is the cause]. Furthermore, the manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the qualities (*guṇas*) cannot occur without a relationship of subordinate and predominant; nor does such a relationship of subordinate and predominant exist without inequality (*vaiṣamya*);
nor does inequality exist without a state of mutual suppression and being suppressed. Thus, there is manifestation in the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others.
Thus ends the second [section].
It might be asked: how can there be a manifold manifestation from qualities that are of a single nature? To this he says:

"(118) The manifestation of the *prakṛti* is like water, due to transformation. For just as water released from a cloud, though of a single taste, assumes various forms upon reaching the modifications of this or that earth; [so too does the *prakṛti*].

It is differentiated by the states of being sweet, sour, salty, bitter, astringent, and pungent, as they ripen through the juices of the coconut, palm, tālī, bilva, cirabilva, tinduka, āmalaka, prācīnāmalaka, and kapittha fruits; thus, from the emergence of each individual quality, the primary qualities set in motion various transformations. This has been stated:
"Due to the distinction based on each respective substratum of the qualities. The meaning is: from that distinction which arises by virtue of each individual quality serving as a substratum. || 16 ||

But as for those who are satisfied with [limited] results (*tauṣṭika*), who— conceiving the unmanifest (*avyakta*), or the great one (*mahat*), or the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), or the senses, or the elements, or the person (*puruṣa*) as the Self— worship those very things, he speaks to them:
This is not a proof.

The Puruṣa exists because the aggregate is for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three guṇas and so forth, because of superintendence, because of the state of being an enjoyer, and because of activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya). || 17 ||
(120) "Because composite entities exist for the sake of another" is the first formal proof.
"Because the composite is for the sake of another. The Puruṣa exists, distinct from the unmanifest (avyakta) and the rest.

Why? "Because the composite is for the sake of another. The unmanifest, the mahat, the ego (ahaṅkāra), and so forth, are for the sake of another, because they are composites, like beds, seats, and the like.
Like ointment and other such things, all composite entities, beginning with the Unmanifest, consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
It might be argued: beds, seats, and so forth are observed to be aggregates for the sake of an embodied being who is a composite; however, the Self is not [an aggregate]. [Ko.
17] (121) [Regarding] aggregates...
If it were for the purpose of being within a composite aggregate, there would be no reversal of the three qualities and so forth.
And whoever...
The proof for the existence of the person (*puruṣa*):

[The argument] that "the sense organs are for another's sake" does not establish anything distinct from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and so forth; therefore, these [reasons] would lead only to another composite entity as the "other," and not to an uncompounded self (*asaṃhata-ātman*).
To this he says: "Because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: if that [Self] were for the sake of another aggregate, then, because it too would be an aggregate, it would have to be for the sake of yet another aggregate; and thus, by that and that, there would be an infinite regress.

It might be argued that when a settled conclusion (*vyavasthā*) exists, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is not logical, because it would entail the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). However, it is not correct to say that "conceptual complexity is tolerated even when supported by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," because the property of being a composite (*saṃhatatva*) is concomitant with mere subservience to another (*pārārthya*) alone. This is seen in the example...

We have demonstrated in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* that for one who desires inference based on conformity with all phenomena (*sarvadharmānurodha*), there follows the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

Therefore, by one who— out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)— desires its non-composite nature (*asaṃghātatva*), its state of not consisting of the three qualities (*atriguṇatva*), its lack of discernment (*avivekitva*), and its being a non-object (*aviṣayatva*) [must be accepted].

You must admit that this [Supreme Being] possesses the qualities of being non-common (asāmānya) and being conscious (cetana), as well as the property of not being productive (aprasavadharmitva). For properties such as consisting of the three guṇas (triguṇatva) are pervaded by the state of being composite (saṃhatatva). Since that state of being composite is excluded from this Supreme Being, it excludes the possession of the three guṇas and so forth, just as the exclusion of being a Brāhmaṇa excludes being a Kaṭha and other such sub-castes. Therefore, the Teacher [said]: "The three guṇas..."
By stating "because of the reversal of [the notions of] 'I' and so forth," it is established that the Supreme, who is uncomposite, is intended, and that He is the Self.

Furthermore, there exists a Puruṣa beyond this [Prakṛti], "because of superintendence" (adhiṣṭhānāt). That which consists of the three guṇas is seen to be superintended by another; for whatever is composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion is observed to be superintended by something else, just as a chariot and so forth are by a driver and so forth.
Since this intellect and so forth consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, they too must be presided over by another; and that other is the Self, which is distinct from the three qualities (guṇas).
The second proof is that those whose nature consists of the three guṇas are presided over [by another]. (2)

For this reason as well, the Puruṣa exists: "because of the state of being an enjoyer. By the state of being an enjoyer, one characterizes the enjoyer with respect to the objects of enjoyment, pleasure and pain. For pleasure and pain, which are to be experienced as favorable and unfavorable respectively, are each individually experienced within oneself. Therefore, by these two... [the existence of the Puruṣa is established]. This is the third [reason]. (3)
There must be something else that is either favorable or unfavorable; however, this does not establish the existence of a multitude of favorable persons. (Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī 38)
The intellect and the other faculties are either to be favored or opposed, because they consist of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
thus, there is a contradiction in their acting upon themselves. Therefore, that which is not essentially of the nature of pleasure and so on is what is to be favored or opposed, and that is the Self.
This is also possible.

Others, however, say: "The objects of experience (*bhogya*), such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, are the visible (*dṛśya*). And without a seer (*draṣṭṛ*), their status as the visible—and their state of being experienced (*bhoktṛbhāva*)—is not logical. Therefore, there exists a seer distinct from the visible intellect and so forth; that is the Self (*ātman*). [This is because] it is due to the existence of a seer that there is the state of being an experiencer.

The meaning is: because of existence, that is, because the seer is inferred from the seen. And the "seen-ness" of the intellect and so forth is inferred from their being of the nature of pleasure and so on, just as it is with earth and the other elements.

For this reason as well, he says that the Puruṣa exists: "And because of the activity of those seeking isolation. The activity of the scriptures, the great seers, and those with divine vision is for the sake of isolation—that is, for the sake of absolute isolation—characterized by the cessation of the threefold suffering; such [cessation] is not possible for the intellect (buddhi) and other [evolutes].
The fourth means of accomplishment—(4).

For how can those things which are essentially suffering and so forth be separated from their own nature? However, for that which is distinct from them and does not possess that nature, separation from it is achievable;

therefore, because of the activity of the scriptures and of the great-minded ones for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*), there exists [a self] distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other factors.
Thus, it is established that there is a self. || 17 ||

(125) Having thus established the existence of the *puruṣa* through the scriptures, a doubt arises as to whether that [puruṣa] is one in all bodies or many— one for each body. (126) To resolve this, its multiplicity in every field (*kṣetra*) is demonstrated.
These are the non-proofs.
The plurality of Puruṣas is established from the specific determination of the causes of birth and death, from their non-simultaneous activity,
and indeed from the diversity of the three guṇas. (18)

By the words beginning with "janana" [the author states]: "The plurality of persons is established. Why? Because of the specific determination of birth and death (janmamaraṇapratiniyamāt); thus, first—
To me (1).
"Because of the specific determination of the causes of birth and death," [it is said]: by means of distinct classes of unprecedented body, sense organs, mind, ego, intellect, and sensations— pu-...

Birth is the connection of the *puruṣa* with *prakṛti*, but not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the *puruṣa* itself, because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). Furthermore, the abandonment of those very bodies and so forth that have been acquired [is due to *prakṛti*]. [This concludes] the proof for the plurality of *puruṣas*. 18] Proof of the plurality of *puruṣas*. Because of its unchangeability, [the *puruṣa* does not undergo transformation]; rather, it is precisely those appropriated things, such as the body and so forth, that are abandoned.

Death is not the destruction of the self, because it is immutable and eternal. The instruments are the thirteen, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*). Regarding these births, deaths, and instruments, there is a fixed distribution. Indeed, this threefold arrangement would not be possible if there were only one person (*puruṣa*) in all bodies. Therefore, there must indeed be many persons in a single body.

If [the self were one], then when one is born, all would be born; when one dies, all would die; if one person were blind and so forth, all would be blind and so forth; and if one were distracted, all would be distracted—thus there would be a lack of order. However, when there is a distinction of persons for each body (*kṣetra*), order is established. Nor is it the case that even for a single [self]...

It is not correct to say that "the distinction [in states] for a person arises from the difference in the bodies assumed," because it would follow that distinctions such as birth and death would also apply due to differences in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) like the hand or the breast; for indeed, when a hand is cut off,
or when a large limb such as a breast is born, a young woman does not thereby become dead or born.
For this reason as well, he states that there is a distinction between persons in each body: "And because of non-simultaneous activity.

Although activity, characterized by effort, resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is nevertheless figuratively attributed to the person (*puruṣa*). Thus, in that regard, within a single body, [there is] effort—

If [the self] were one, then since that very same [self] would be one in all bodies, it would exert effort everywhere, and consequently, it would move all bodies simultaneously. However, if there is plurality [of selves], this fault does not arise.

For this reason as well, he states that there is a distinction between persons: "And because of the reversal of the three qualities" (*traiguṇyaviparyayāccaiva*). The particle *eva* (indeed) is displaced [from its position] after *siddham* (established); it should be understood as following that word.
This is the third [reason]. It is established, not unestablished. The three qualities are *traiguṇya*; of that...

"Viparyaya" means "alteration. Indeed, some classes of beings abound in *sattva*, such as the gods; some abound in *rajas*, such as human beings; and some abound in *tamas*, such as those in the animal realm.
This very alteration, this transformation consisting of the reversal of the three *guṇas*, exists among those classes of beings.
This would be a fault if there were only one person; however, when there is a plurality of persons, this is not a defect. || 18 ||
(128) "Because the activities of persons do not occur simultaneously"— this is the second [reason]. (2)

(130) The Attributes of the Puruṣa: Having thus established the plurality of Puruṣas, he states their attributes for the sake of their utility in discriminative knowledge— this is the "Exposition of the Attributes of the Puruṣa."
And from this absence of error, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation, neutrality, the state of being a seer, and the absence of agency. (19)
And from that [verse], "ca" (and) conjoins other attributes along with the plurality of the Puruṣas.
If it were said, "from this error," it would be connected to what was immediately mentioned before—namely, "from the reversal of the three guṇas"; therefore...

To eliminate this doubt, the word "tasmāt" (therefore) was stated. For that which was mentioned immediately prior is the referent of "idam" (this) due to proximity, whereas "tat" (that) refers to what is remote; thus, the remote qualities—namely, "consisting of the three guṇas," "non-discriminative," and so forth—are connected [to "tat"].

Therefore, that which is the reverse of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth constitutes for the *puruṣa* the state of being devoid of the three qualities, discriminative awareness, the state of not being an object, uniqueness, sentience, and the quality of non-procreativity. Among these,
by means of sentience and the state of not being an object, its status as the witness (*sākṣin*) and the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) is demonstrated.
For it is the conscious one who is the seer, not the unconscious; and the witness is one to whom an object has been shown.

He to whom the object is presented is the witness; for in the world, the plaintiff and the defendant show the subject matter of their dispute to the witness, and in the same way, primordial nature (prakṛti) shows its own activity.

Because it shows the object to the Puruṣa, the Puruṣa is the witness; neither the insentient nor the object itself is capable of showing the object. Thus, by virtue of its sentience and its non-objectivity, it becomes the witness; for this very reason, it is also the seer.
Therefore, there is the demonstration of the relationship of the word.
[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī (132)] The Puruṣa is the witness because of his being devoid of the three guṇas and so forth.
And the state of being a seer.

And because of its being devoid of the three *guṇas*, it possesses isolation (*kaivalya*). Isolation is the absolute absence of the threefold suffering. (133) That isolation is established for it precisely because of its natural state of being devoid of the three *guṇas*, that is, because it is free from pleasure, pain, and delusion.

For this very reason, due to the absence of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), there is neutrality (*mādhyasthya*). For one who is happy is satisfied by happiness, and one who is suffering hates suffering; thus, such a person does not become neutral. But one who is devoid of both is called "neutral" (*madhyastha*) and "indifferent" (*udāsīna*).
Because it is discriminative and because it lacks the nature of productivity, it is established that [the Self] is not the agent. || 19 ||
And there is the state of being a non-agent.

It might be argued: "Having understood the object to be accomplished through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the conscious one thinks, 'I, being desirous of acting, act'—[this is] the conscious agent. [Kośa 20–21] (135) Consciousness and agency.
The doubt regarding the contingency of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya) with respect to itself.
(136) This is an accepted consequence:
the cognition of coreferentiality is a manifestation of error.
Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient;
and likewise, although the Guṇas are the actual agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent. (20)

"Therefore" means: since it has been established through reasoning that consciousness and agency reside in different substrates, therefore this [notion] is an error. He will later describe the "mark" (liṅga), which extends from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the subtle elements; that is the seed of the error.
Yoga is proximity to that. The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. || 20 ||
"The conjunction of the Puruṣa and Pradhāna.
Thus, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of agency and consciousness is established by experience;
however, this is not possible in this [Sāṃkhya] system, because the conscious being is not an agent.
Because the agent is insentient, he says:
"From its conjunction" (*tatsaṃyogāt*). Furthermore, a conjunction between two distinct things does not occur without mutual dependence;
nor can there be such a relationship between the Puruṣa and Pradhāna without a relation of benefitter and benefited. Thus, he [proceeds to] state the cause of this dependence.
There is doubt regarding their conjunction.
He states the purpose [of creation]: "For the sake of seeing the Puruṣa, and likewise for the sake of isolation (kaivalya) of Pradhāna;
the conjunction of both is like that of the lame and the blind, and from that, creation proceeds. (21)
(138) The primary cause's dependence on the person is its dependence on the enjoyer.

Regarding the phrase "of the person" (*puruṣasya*): the genitive case here is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). It means that the perception of *pradhāna*, the universal cause, is for the sake of the person. By this, the fact that *pradhāna* is an object of experience (*bhogyatā*) is demonstrated. Consequently, *pradhāna* is the object of experience and [the person] is the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*).
Since [the experience] is not possible without an enjoyer, its dependence upon an enjoyer is logical.

He shows the Puruṣa’s dependence [on the Pradhāna] with the words: “for the sake of the Puruṣa’s isolation (kaivalya). For indeed, the Puruṣa, being conjoined with the Pradhāna—which exists for the sake of isolation—imagines the threefold suffering inherent in that [Pradhāna] to belong to his own self and thus seeks isolation. And that [isolation] consists of the [Puruṣa’s] pure...

Error regarding the distinction between the *sattva* (the intellect) and the *puruṣa* (the self) is the cause [of bondage]. Nor can the discernment of the distinction between *sattva* and *puruṣa* exist without the *pradhāna*.
The meaning is that the categories contained within the *kārikās* are indeed clear. [This concludes] the explanation of the sequence of creation.
[Sāṃkhya-tantra]:

"The Puruṣa requires Pradhāna for the sake of isolation (kaivalya). And because the succession of conjunctions is beginningless, it is logical that even though he was conjoined for the sake of experience, he is conjoined again for the sake of isolation."

Now, one might ask: "Granted that there is a conjunction of the two [the Puruṣa and Prakṛti], but from what does the creation of Mahat and the rest arise? To this he says: "Creation is produced by that [conjunction]. For the conjunction alone is not sufficient for experience or for liberation without the creation of Mahat and the rest; thus, it is the conjunction itself [that brings about creation].
The meaning is that He creates for the sake of experience and liberation. || 21 ||
(140) The creation of the great principle (mahat) and the subsequent evolutes is necessarily required solely for the sake of experience and liberation.

He states the order of creation: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise. (22)
Regarding the phrase "from *prakṛti*": *prakṛti* is the unmanifest (*avyakta*). *Mahat* and *ahaṅkāra* have their characteristics to be described later.

From *prakṛti* comes *mahat*; from *mahat* come the eleven organs to be described and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as sound and the rest—this is the sequence of creation. This group, limited to sixteen in number, is the "sixteenfold."
Śaka: From those five subtle elements (tanmātras) as well, which have been further withdrawn from the group of sixteen, the five gross elements beginning with space arise.

In that regard, from the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) arises space, which has sound as its quality; from the subtle elements beginning with the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), accompanied by the subtle element of sound, arises air, which has sound and touch as its qualities. Thus, the creation of the elements proceeds according to the sequence of qualities of the subtle elements of sound and touch. From the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*), accompanied by the subtle elements of sound and touch, arises fire, which has sound, touch, and form as its qualities. Sound—
From the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), accompanied by the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), water arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste.

From the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), accompanied by the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, and taste, earth arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; such is the meaning. || 22 ||

The unmanifest (*avyakta*) has been characterized generally by the statement, “That which is the opposite of that [is the unmanifest]” (Kārikā 10), and specifically by the statement, “Sattva is light and illuminating” (Kārikā 13). The manifest (*vyakta*) is also [characterized] generally—
Introduction.
[Verse 23] The definition of the intellect (*buddhi*) and its attributes have already been characterized by the passage beginning with "having a cause" (*hetumat*, Verse 10). Now, however—
He defines the intellect (*buddhi*), distinguished as manifest, because it is useful for the knowledge of discrimination:
"Intellect is determination; virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power—this is its form when characterized by *sattva*; when characterized by *tamas*, it is the opposite of this. (23)

Regarding the term "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*): "Ascertainment is intellect" (*buddhi*)—this is the definition of intellect intended [here] by way of the non-difference between the action and the agent of the action. Every practical agent, having reflected and thought, [says]: "I am ascertainment."

It is established in common worldly experience that one who has been appointed [to a task], having reflected "this must be done by me," resolves upon it and then proceeds to act. In this context, that determination which consists of the judgment "this is to be done" belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*), which has acquired consciousness through its proximity to consciousness (*cit*); it is the unique function of the intellect.

The cognition is non-different from that [object]; and that [non-difference] is the defining characteristic of cognition, because it serves to exclude [the object] from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes.

Having thus examined the intellect (*buddhi*), he describes its sattvic qualities—which are conducive to discriminative knowledge—as follows: “Dharma, knowledge, non-attachment, and sovereignty—these are the sattvic qualities;
dharma and knowledge consist of this form, while that which is contrary to this is tamasic. Dharma...
These are designated as passion and sovereignty.

Among them, dharma, knowledge, and dispassion are the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Therein, dharma—produced by the performance of sacrifices, gifts, and so forth—is the cause of worldly prosperity; [dharma] produced by the practice of the eightfold yoga is...
Homage.

And the cause of the supreme good has been set forth: discriminative knowledge of the difference between the qualities (guṇa) and the person (puruṣa) is knowledge; dispassion is detachment, the absence of passion.
For him— there is the perception of striving (yatamāna-saṃjñā),
which is the mastery over the senses through the exclusion of striving in the state of detachment (virāga).
There are four designations according to their causal forms.

The four notions (saṃjñā) are: the notion of detachment (vyatireka-saṃjñā), the notion of unity (ekendriya-saṃjñā), and the notion of mastery (vaśīkāra-saṃjñā). The impurities (kaṣāya) such as passion (rāga) and the like reside within the mind;
by means of them, the senses are set in motion toward their respective objects. Therefore...

The application of effort for the sake of maturing those [faculties] so that the sense organs might function within their respective objects is the "perception of striving" (*yatamāna-saṃjñā*). While this maturation is being carried out, some of the defilements (*kaṣāya*) have been matured, while others are yet to be matured; such being the sequence of prior and subsequent stages, from among those [defilements] yet to be matured—

The determination of those [factors] as distinct from the "matured" (pakva) is the designation of "the excluded" (vyatireka). These are the attributes of the intellect (buddhi) due to its incapacity for the functioning of the senses, as well as the characteristic of egoism (ahaṅkāra). [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī:
The establishment of the matured factors in the mind by means of mere eagerness is the designation of "single-sensed" (ekendriya). Mere eagerness—

The cessation of even that [desire] while perceptible and scriptural objects are present, which is beyond the three types of cognition, is the cognition of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*). Regarding this, the venerable Patañjali described it: "Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the cognition of mastery in one who is free from thirst for perceptible and scriptural objects" (Yoga Sūtra 1.15).
Thus, this dispassion is a property of the intellect.

Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is also a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*), from which the manifestation of *aṇimā* and the other [powers] occurs. (1) Here, *aṇimā* is the state of becoming subtle, established as a form of sovereignty, by which one enters even into a stone. (2) *Laghimā* is the state of lightness, by which, having taken hold of the rays of the sun, one reaches the world of the sun. [This concludes] the description of the eight perfections (*siddhis*). (147) *Sūryalokam* (the world of the sun).

(3) *Garimā* is the state of heaviness, from which one becomes heavy. (4) *Mahimā* is the state of greatness, from which one becomes great. (5) *Prāpti* is the power by which one touches the moon with the tip of a finger.
(6) *Prākāmya* is the non-obstruction of desire, by which one emerges from and sinks into the earth as if in water.

(7) Mastery (*vaśitva*), by which the primary elements and their derivatives necessarily come under one's control; lordship (*īśitva*), by which one exercises authority over the origin and maintenance of the primary elements and their derivatives; and (8) the power of determining objects at will (*kāmacārāvasāyitva*), which is the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*), whereby the elements become exactly as his resolve regarding them intends—unlike that of other human beings.
Resolutions conform to the objects to be resolved; however, for the yogi, the objects to be resolved conform to the resolution.
These are the four sattvic qualities of the intellect.
The qualities of darkness (tamas) pertaining to the intellect (buddhi) are unrighteousness (adharma) and so forth.

The qualities of the intellect belonging to *tamas*, however, are the opposite of those; the meaning is that they are fourfold, designated as unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). || 23 ||
He states the definition of egoism (ahaṅkāra): "Egoism is self-conceit; from it proceeds a twofold creation:
the group of eleven and the five subtle elements. (24)

Regarding the term "abhimāna": "abhimāna" is the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense). For that which has been perceived and reflected upon, there arises within the *ahaṅkāra* the notions: "I am authorized here," "I am indeed capable in this matter," "these objects are for my sake alone," and "there is no one else here but me."
The definition.
[Regarding Gkau. 24–25:
The specific effects of *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense).
That conceit which thinks, "Someone has been insulted by me," or "Therefore, I exist"—that is the uncommon [function].
The ego (ahaṅkāra) exists because it is the agent of activity; for, depending upon that [ego], the intellect (buddhi) determines and forms the resolve: "This must be done by me."
He states the distinction of its effects: "From that, the twofold creation proceeds. He states the two types:
"The group of eleven, and [the group] consisting of five."
And the five subtle elements; by the word "only" (eva), he restricts [the meaning] to indicate that the creation from the ego (ahaṅkāra) is indeed of these two kinds and no other. || 24 ||
(150) The different effects of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
This might be the case:
how can the group [of faculties] that illuminates the insentient and the two distinct [entities] arise from a single-natured cause such as the *ahaṅkāra*? To this, he says:
The group of eleven [senses] proceeds from the modified (vaikṛta) ego as sattvic;
from the elemental (bhūtādi) [ego] comes the subtle elements (tanmātra), which is tamasic; and from the fiery (taijasa) [ego] come both. (25)

Regarding the term "sāttvika": the group of eleven faculties, characterized by luminosity and lightness, proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (modified) ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as *sāttvika*. From the *bhūtādi* (elemental-origin) ego, however, the group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*, proceeds. Why? Because [the text says] "of the *sattva* and *tamas*."
(151) Although the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is of a single form, there are various modifications due to the differentiation of its qualities (*guṇa*); from *sattva*, the sense organs (*indriya*) arise.
From the tamasic [aspect], the group of subtle elements (tanmātra) arises.
The purposefulness of *rajas* consists in its being the initiator of both *sattva* and *tamas*.
This is what is meant: although the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is one, it nevertheless performs distinct functions due to the emergence and suppression of the various qualities (guṇas).
Now, if all effects are produced by *sattva* and *tamas* alone, then what is the use of *rajas*, which would be rendered ineffective?
To this he says: “From the *taijasa* (the passionate), both [arise]. From the *taijasa*—that is, from *rajas*—both groups [of organs] arise. Although [it may seem that] *rajas*...

There is no other effect [of rajas]; nevertheless, although sattva and tamas are inherently inactive and capable [in themselves], they do not perform their respective effects; rather, when rajas, by virtue of its mobility, impels them, then they perform their own effects. Thus, in both types of effects, [the agency belongs] to sattva and tamas.
Since rajas possesses causality by way of producing activity, rajas is not useless. || 25 ||
The ten external organs.
To explain the eleventh as being composed of *sattva*, he first states the ten external organs:
the sense organs of cognition (the *buddhīndriyas*) are those called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin.
They say that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action (karmendriyas). || 26 ||
Regarding the phrase "the sense organs of cognition" (*buddhīndriyāṇi*): the nature of a sense organ (*indriyatva*) consists in being derived from *sāttvika* food.

Furthermore, (153) the external sense organs are of two kinds: the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Both of these constitute a group of ten. They are called "sense organs" (*indriya*) because they are the marks (*cihna*) of the Self (*indra*). And these—
And the origin of the world.

They are designated by their own names, such as "eye" and so forth. Among them, the eye is that which has the apprehension of form as its characteristic; the ear is that which has the apprehension of sound as its characteristic; the nose is that which has the apprehension of odor as its characteristic; the tongue is that which has the apprehension of taste as its characteristic; and the skin is that which has the apprehension of touch as its characteristic—these are the designations for the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). Thus...
He will describe the function of speech and the other [organs] in verse 28.
[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī states the eleventh sense organ:
Here, the mind (manas) is of a dual nature; it is both the faculty of volition (saṅkalpaka) and a sense organ (indriya) due to its common characteristics.
The diversity [of the intellect] arises from the specific transformation of the guṇas and from external distinctions. || 27 ||
"Of a dual nature. Among the eleven sense organs, the mind (*manas*) is of a dual nature;

for the mind is both a cognitive faculty (*buddhīndriya*) and an organ of action (*karmendriya*). This establishes the dual nature of the mind in relation to the eyes and so forth, as well as the voice and so forth, because it is only when presided over by the mind that they engage with their respective objects.
He defines it by its specific characteristic: "In this context, the mind is that which conceives. The mind is characterized by the form of conception (*saṅkalpa*). [The text continues:
"That which has been perceived by the sense organ is [the object] of the mind...
(155) [This is the definition of the mind.]

The state of being characterized by mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) is the indistinct [cognition] that "this is an object," as well as the synthesis (*samanvaya*) [of thought] such as "this is thus" or "it is not thus."
Thus he correctly conceptualizes; that is to say, he discriminates by means of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. As they have said:
"First, one perceives the mere object in its undifferentiated and unconceptualized state."
"Therefore, the wise conceptualize it through both the universal and the particular. Thus [it is said].

For instance, there is indeed an initial non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition of mere observation, arising from an object that is as if deluded, similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth. Subsequently, however, by means of which [cognition] the object is [grasped] through its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and the like...

That [object] too is determined by the intellect (buddhi), and it is accepted as being directly perceived (pratyakṣa). This operation of the mind, characterized by conceptual construction (saṅkalpa), defines the mind by distinguishing it from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes.

It might be argued: just as the *mahat* and the *ahaṅkāra*, being associated with unique functions, are not sense organs (*indriya*), so too the *manas*, being associated with a unique function, ought not to be a sense organ. To this he says: "And it is a sense organ. Why?

"Because of similarity. The similarity with other sense organs consists in having the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as their material cause; it does not consist in being a mark of Indra (*indraliṅgatva*), for otherwise the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego would also follow as being sense organs by virtue of being marks of the Self (*ātman*). Therefore, being a mark of Indra consists merely in originating from him.
But it is not the ground for the application [of the term].

Now, as to how the eleven organs arise from a single *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), it is said: "The diversity [of the organs] and their external distinctions result from the specific transformation of the *guṇas*.
This is because of the difference in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that acts as a concomitant cause for the engagement in the experience of sound and other objects, which constitutes the effect.
Difference [is explained]. Even the difference of the unperceived is simply a transformation of the *guṇas*.
The phrase "and external differences" is for the sake of an illustration—the meaning being that just as there are external differences, so too is this [internal difference]. || 27 ||
(156) Proof of the mind’s status as a sense organ: its inclusion among the senses by the Sāttvika ego.
Because of the common characteristic of having the nature of being characterized by generosity.
(157) The diversity of effects arises from the specific transformation of the qualities within a single *ahaṃkāra*.
(158) And the phrase "and external distinctions" is for the purpose of providing an illustration.
(159) An Exposition of the Functions of the Ten Faculties.
Thus, having described the eleven organs according to their essential nature, he states the specific, non-common functions of ten of them:
"The function of the five [sensory organs] with respect to sound and the other objects is held to be mere perception."
And speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the five [elements]. (28)

The perception of an indistinct object by the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) is called *ālocana* (observation). "Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the five [organs]" refers to the organs of action (*karmendriya*). The organ located in the throat, palate, and other places is speech;
its function is speaking. The functions of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) are clear. (28)48
He states the function of the three internal organs:
"The specific characteristic is the function of the triad; this is its uncommon [function].
The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa. (29)
The functions of the internal organs.

Regarding the term "specific nature" (*svālakṣaṇyam*): this is the specific nature of the triad of functions. Those whose characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are their own (*sva*), not shared with others, are the "specific natures" (*svalakṣaṇa*); these are the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*). Of these—

(160) The state of the three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of their respective specific characteristics is *svālakṣaṇya*; and that consists of their own respective characteristics, namely, the three unique functions (*vṛtti*).
It is as follows: the great [intellect] has the function of intense attachment; egoity has the function of the five forms of wind;
and the unmanifest has the common function of all.
[Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī] Self-conceit (abhimāna), volition (saṅkalpa), is the modification (vṛtti) or activity (vyāpāra) of the mind (manas).

He states the twofold nature of the functions by way of their being common and uncommon: "This very [function] is uncommon and specific; the function of the general organs is that which begins with prāṇa."
"The five vital airs (vāyavaḥ). This function of the instruments is common [to all].

For all three types of instruments, the five vital airs constitute the life-function (*jīvana-vṛtti*), because they exist when those [airs] are present and cease to exist when they are absent. Among them, *prāṇa* functions in the tip of the nose, the heart, the navel, and the big toe; *apāna* [functions] in the throat...

The five vital airs (vāyu) are as follows: prāṇa functions in the mouth, nose, feet, anus, genitals, and sides; samāna functions in the heart, navel, and all the joints; udāna functions in the heart, throat, palate, head, and the space between the eyebrows; and vyāna functions in the skin. || 29 ||
He states the simultaneous and successive operations of this fourfold instrument, along with their specific modes, within its unique functions:
"The operation of the fourfold [instrument] is both simultaneous and successive;
however, regarding the perceived, it is likewise [simultaneous], while regarding the unperceived, the operation of the three is preceded by that [perception]. (30)

Regarding the term "simultaneously" (*yugapat*): as observed in experience— for instance, when one sees a four-tusked elephant or a tiger directly in front, very close at hand, amidst a pitch-black darkness accompanied by a flash of lightning—

then the functions of perception (*ālocana*), conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), self-identification (*abhimāna*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*) occur simultaneously within this [cognition] in direct perception.
Wherever they appear, having leaped up from that very spot, he steps away from that place in a single stride.

And as for the sequence: when, in dim light, one first perceives the mere object in a vague manner, and then gradually—having fixed the mind—the hands draw the bowstring back to the ear with an arrow;
[this is] the mutual dependence of the instruments. [Kārikās 30–31]
He perceives that this is an exceedingly fierce thief with his bow drawn into a circle; yet he thinks, "He is approaching me," and then resolves, "I shall depart from this place."

Regarding the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), however, he states that the function of the three internal organs—excluding the external senses—is preceded by perception: “In the case of the unperceived, the function of the triad of internal organs is preceded by perception” (YS 1.7). This means that for the triad of internal organs, there are two types of functions regarding the imperceptible: those occurring simultaneously and those occurring sequentially, both of which are preceded by perception. [These consist of] inference, scripture, and memory.
It is exactly as it was seen before.
For three [means of knowledge] operate regarding an imperceptible object preceded by perception, and not otherwise; the application is that as it was seen, so it is in the unseen as well. (30)

It might be argued as follows: the activities of the four or three [internal organs] do not depend on those [objects] alone; for if they were eternal instruments, it would follow that their activities must arise at all times due to their own inherent nature. Furthermore, if they were accidental, there would be the consequence of a confusion of activities due to the absence of any cause for restriction. To this, he says:
The defects in the state of being a tantra.
Each [organ] resorts to its own respective function, which has as its cause the mutual impelling [of one another];
the purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause, for no instrument is set in motion by anything else.

"Belonging to oneself"—the word "instruments" (*karaṇāni*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. For just as many men—(166) namely, those armed with spears, clubs, bows, and swords—who have made a mutual agreement, engage in battle for the purpose of attacking the enemy while depending upon one another; therein, having understood the intention of one among them...

Regarding the instruments [of action] in their respective functions: one or another [instrument] proceeds; and when it proceeds, the wielder of the spear (*śāktika*) takes up only the spear, not the staff or other implements, and likewise the wielder of the staff (*yāṣṭika*) takes up only the staff, not the spear or others. Thus, by the intention (*ākūta*) of one particular instrument—that is, its orientation toward performing its own specific task—one particular instrument [is employed].
It proceeds; and because it is the cause of that proceeding, there is no contingency of a confusion of functions, as it has been stated: "each attains its own [function]."
It might be argued:

"The staff-bearer and others, being sentient, proceed after having understood each other's intentions"— whether this refers to the external sense organs assisted by the mind, or to the three internal organs.
[This is] incorrect.

For the instruments (*karaṇa*) are insentient; therefore, even though they possess their own nature, they are not capable of acting toward the purpose of the *puruṣa* without being directed by a supervisor. Thus, there must be a supervisor for these instruments. Their essential nature—
Or rather, it is the state of being a motivator.
One must possess mastery over the application of this capacity; therefore, he says:

"The purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha) is the motivator, and there is a differentiation of instruments. "The purpose of the Spirit alone is the cause; the instrument is not set in motion by anything else. [This refers to] enjoyment and liberation.

The moment (*kṣaṇa*), being the very purpose of the Person (*puruṣārtha*) while still in a future state, sets the instruments into motion; there is no need here for an agent who knows its own nature. And this will be demonstrated in the commentary on the verse beginning with "for the sake of the calf's growth" (Kārikā 57). || 31 ||
(168) The Division of the Instruments of Action.
It has been stated that "the instrument is not caused by anything. Therein, he analyzes the instrument:
the instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of seizing, retaining, and manifesting.
And its function is tenfold: that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be maintained, and that which is to be manifested. || 32 ||

"The instrument (*karaṇa*) is of thirteen kinds. This means that the eleven sense organs (*indriya*), along with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), constitute the thirteenfold instrument. An instrument is a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka*). Since there can be no status as a causal factor without the entry of activity (*vyāpārāveśa*), [activity is required]. [The enumeration of the instruments follows: * **The five organs of perception** (*buddhīndriya*): the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. * **The five organs of action** (*karmendriya*): speech, hands, feet, the organ of excretion, and the organ of generation. * **The internal instruments** (*antaḥkaraṇa*): the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Thus, the instruments are enumerated as thirteen. An instrument is defined as a specific causal factor (*kāraka-viśeṣa*). And since there is no status as a causal factor without the application of activity, [activity is necessarily involved].

Rāva explains: “It performs the functions of taking up, retaining, and manifesting,” as is appropriate. In this regard, the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, perform the function of taking up (*āharanti*); that is to say, they grasp their respective objects and pervade them through their own specific operations.
The intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*), however, sustain (*dhārayanti*) things by means of their own activity characterized as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
The sense organs illuminate.

Since actions such as bringing (*āharaṇa*) and holding (*dhāraṇa*) are transitive (*sakarmaka*), one might ask: what is the object (*karman*), and how many kinds are there? To this, [the author] says: "And its effect (*kārya*)," thereby enumerating three types of objects.

The tenfold instrument [of action] is tenfold: that which is to be acquired (*āhārya*), that which is to be sustained (*dhārya*), and that which is to be manifested (*prakāśya*). "To be acquired" means that which is to be pervaded (*vyāpya*). For the organs of action, speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation are their respective objects of pervasion; and these, being either divine or non-divine as the case may be, constitute the ten—this is "that which is to be acquired."
The meaning is "in due order. [Cko.
32-33] There is a further internal division within the thirteenfold instrument (karaṇa).
Or rather, ten. Likewise, the body is supported by the three internal instruments through their functions characterized as prāṇa and so forth.
And that [body] consists of the five elements, beginning with earth. Earth is the aggregate of the five [qualities], sound and so forth;

and since these five are both divine and non-divine, they are to be understood as tenfold. Likewise, for the sense organs, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective objects; and these too are, respectively, either divine or non-divine.
"Ten" refers to that which is to be manifested as the tenfold [group]. || 32 ||
(171) The intermediate subdivision within the thirteenfold classification is due to the distinction between the external and the internal.
The internal organ is threefold, while the external is tenfold; it is called the object of the [internal] triad.
The external organ functions in the present time, whereas the internal organ functions across the three times.
(172) The threefold nature of the internal organ.
He makes an internal subdivision within the thirteenfold instrument: the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇas) pertain to all three times.

Regarding the term "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*): the internal organ is threefold—namely, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*). It is called the "internal organ" because it exists within the body.

The tenfold external instrument is called the "object" of the threefold internal instrument. (173) It makes known the external object; it serves as a gateway for the functions of objective determination, conceptualization, self-identification, and ascertainment that must be performed. Among these, the organs of cognition—
The [other] natures consist of ten elements.
By speech, however, the organs of action [are satisfied] by their respective functions.

He states another distinction between the external and internal instruments: "pertaining to the present time. The external sense organ has as its object the present time. The proximity to the present—whether future or even past—is also considered present for the external instrument; therefore, speech too pertains to the present time.
The present time does not become an object [of inference]. As it is said: "The internal instrument [functions] across the three times.
For example: from the swelling of a river's flood, it follows that there *was* rain; there *is* [rain]; [there will be rain].
The ellipsis is "they become [the means of] flowing. [Sāṃkhya-tattva-kaumudī, Chapter 1, Verse 52:
Analysis of the Instruments and their Objects.]

From smoke, one infers fire here in the mountain thicket; from the movement of ant eggs, even in the absence of any visible obstacle, one infers that it will rain; and there arise corresponding volitions, self-identifications, and determinations.

Furthermore, the single time (*kāla*) as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas is not capable of producing the various linguistic usages such as "future" and so forth. Therefore, those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) by which this [time] is understood to have distinctions such as "future" and so on— without being a different entity [from time itself]— let them be the very means for the linguistic usage of "future" and so forth.

The teachers of Sāṃkhya hold that time is merely a cause for the manifestation [of effects]; what is the use here of this superfluous entity (antargaḍu) called time? Therefore, there is no acceptance of time as a distinct ontological principle (tattva). || 33 ||
(176) The analysis of the objects of the external sense-faculties.
He distinguishes the objects of the external sense organs pertaining to the present time:
"Of those, the five sense organs have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific."
Speech has sound as its object; the remaining [senses], however, have five objects. || 34 ||

Regarding the phrase "the organs of cognition" (*buddhīndriyāṇi*): among those ten—namely, the five organs of cognition and the [five] organs of action—"five" [of them] are [those that perceive] the specific and non-specific [objects]. (177) [The text continues: "...specific and non-specific..."

The objects (*viṣaya*) consist of gross and subtle forms. Regarding the objects: the "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) are the gross [elements] such as sound and so forth, appearing as calm, fierce, or delusive, and having the nature of earth and the other elements; the "non-particulars" (*aviśeṣa*) are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the subtle [forms] of sound and so forth. By the inclusion of the term "subtle," he excludes the gross elements. Both particulars and non-particulars are "particular-non-particulars" (*viśeṣāviśeṣa*).

Those sense organs whose objects are these [respective] elements are described as such. Among them, for those yogins who possess the upward stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the ear has both the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) and gross sound as its object; however, for people like us, it has only gross sound as its object. In this same way, their skin has both gross and subtle touch as its object, whereas for people like us, it has only gross touch as its object.

However, it has only coarse touch as its object. In the same way, the eyes and the other [senses] of those beings, as well as those of people like us, should be understood with respect to subtle and coarse forms and so forth.

Thus, among the organs of action, "speech has sound as its object," meaning it has gross sound as its object; [this occurs] at the stage of the subtle element (*tanmātra*). [Note: There is an alternative reading, *'bhūtabhāvināvapākaroti'* (it removes both the past and the future). [Kau.
34–35–36] The predominance of the internal organs.
The objects of the senses.
(178) However, it is not the cause of the sound-tanmātra, because that [sound-tanmātra] is derived from the *ahaṃkāra* and thus shares a single cause with the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*).
As for the "remaining four"—namely, those called the anus, the genitals, the hands, and the feet—they have five objects; [the object] of the hand is—
Because composite objects such as jars and the like consist of the five [elements], beginning with sound. || 34 ||
Now, he states with reasons the predominant status of certain [instruments] among the thirteen instruments:
"Since the intellect, together with the internal organs, perceives all objects, therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates. (35)
"With the internal organ" (*sāntaḥkaraṇā*): "the gate" (*dvāri*) refers to *pradhāna*. "The gates" (*dvārāṇi*) are the organs;

the external sense-organs are the gates. Through them, everything brought forward in the encounters [with objects] becomes the object of the internal organs. For it is from this that the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the mind (*manas*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), penetrates.
Grain.
Therefore, the external sense organs are the doors, and the intellect (buddhi), together with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), possesses those doors. || 35 ||

The intellect (*buddhi*) is not only primary in relation to the external sense organs, but it is also primary even in relation to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind (*manas*), which act as gatekeepers; thus he says:
"These specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*), though distinct from one another, are like lamps."
Having illuminated the entire purpose of the person, they present it to the intellect. || 36 ||

Regarding the word “these”: just as a district magistrate, having collected taxes from the householders, delivers them to the superintendent of the interior treasury, and the superintendent of the [interior] treasury delivers them to the superintendent of the realm, and he in turn to the king; so too do the external senses, having performed their preliminary observation (*ālocana*), [deliver the data to the internal organ]. Furthermore, among all the organs, the intellect (*buddhi*) holds primacy.

They offer [the objects] to the mind; the mind, having formed a conceptualization, offers them to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and the ego-sense, having determined them, offers them to the intellect (buddhi), which serves as the presiding authority over all.
Thus it has been said: "Having illuminated the object for the person (puruṣa), they present it to the intellect."

The external senses, the mind, and the ego are "particular manifestations of the *guṇas*"; that is, [they are manifestations] of the *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—even though these *guṇas* are by nature mutually antagonistic.
(180) Even for *guṇas* whose dispositions are opposed to one another...
The single activity, which consists of the human goal, is like a lamp.
But why do they present [the objects] to the intellect (*buddhi*), and not to the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) which is the gatekeeper, nor to the mind (*manas*)? To this he says:
"The intellect has primacy over all."

[Sāṃkhya-tattva-vikārāḥ: These modifications (vikāras), although by nature mutually opposed, are brought into a state of syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) by the purpose of the Puruṣa, namely experience (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga); just as, for example, in the case of a lamp-wick—

Just as water, fire, and wind, having combined for the purpose of illuminating form by removing total darkness, constitute a lamp, so too are these specific qualities; such is the construction [of the analogy]. || 36 ||
Since it is the intellect that accomplishes all experience for the puruṣa, and it is that same intellect which again distinguishes the subtle difference between the pradhāna and the puruṣa. (37)

Regarding the word “all”: because the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the motivator, that which is its direct means is the primary means for the intellect (*buddhi*). And since the intellect is its direct means, it alone is the primary [means]—the direct instrument for the human goal. Just as the superintendent of all is the direct instrument for the king’s purpose.

Because it is the means of accomplishing the purpose (*arthasādhanatvāt*). By virtue of being the means, it is primary; however, others such as the village overseer and so forth are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to it. For the intellect (*buddhi*), through its proximity to the *puruṣa* and by assuming its reflection, becomes as if of that same nature and accomplishes for the *puruṣa* the enjoyment of all objects. Indeed, experience (*bhoga*) is the perception of pleasure and pain, and that—

In the intellect (*buddhi*), and since the intellect is indeed of the nature of the *puruṣa*, it causes the *puruṣa* to experience [objects]. Just as the withdrawal of objects, volition, and self-conceit, having entered the intellect through transformations into their respective forms, so too do the operations of the sense organs become co-operative with the determination (*adhyavasāya*)— which is the very operation of the intellect— just as, for example:

The army of the village headman and others, together with his own troops, belongs to the supreme commander. [Likewise,] that which is the "enjoyment" of the "Person" (puruṣa) "with regard to" all objects such as sound and so forth, he brings about.
Now, if the intellect is that which effects the enjoyment of all objects for the person (puruṣa), then [the person] would never be liberated;
therefore, he says: subsequently, it "distinguishes" the specific [object].
