However, when those whose fruition has already begun are exhausted through experience, then "when the separation from the body has been reached" means upon its destruction; and "because its purpose has been fulfilled" means because its function has been accomplished.

When the primary cause (pradhāna) ceases its activity toward that person (puruṣa), the person attains both "absolute" (*aikāntika*)— meaning necessarily occurring— and "ultimate" (*ātyantika*)— meaning indestructible— "isolation" (*kaivalya*), which is the departure from the threefold suffering. || 68 ||
(275) The fact that the Sāṃkhya treatise was composed by the Supreme Sage.
Even though it has been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states that it was preceded by the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*) in order to generate absolute faith:
"This secret knowledge of the goal of human life was fully proclaimed by the Supreme Sage."
In this [treatise], the persistence, origin, and dissolution of living beings are investigated. || 69 ||
Regarding the term "Puruṣa": it is "secret" (*guhya*), meaning it dwells in a cave (*guhā-nivāsin*), that is to say, it is difficult for those of dull intellect to understand.
By the phrase "by the supreme seer" (*paramarṣiṇā*), [the author] refers to Kapila; he strengthens that very faith by establishing its scriptural authority (*āgamikatva*) with the words:

"In which the stability, origin, and dissolution of beings are contemplated. "In which" means in that knowledge—for the sake of which—[is this treatise composed]. [This concludes] the authoritative validity of the Sāṃkhya scripture. (Kau. 69–70–71–72) 81.
Just as it is said, "One kills the leopard for its skin," the "abiding, arising, and dissolution of beings"—that is, of living creatures—are "contemplated" through the scriptures. || 69 ||
It might be argued:
"That which was taught directly by the Supreme Seer [the Buddha],
starting from Kapila down to Pañcaśikha..."
We shall believe that; furthermore, regarding what was stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa therein (276),
[it concerns] the lineage of teacher and disciple in the Sāṃkhya school.
It has been explained.
Whence comes faith? To this he says:
The Sage gave this to Āsuri out of compassion; it is pure and immortal.
Āsuri [taught] it to Pañcaśikha, and by him the tantra was made manifold.

Regarding the word "this" (*etat*) in the verse: "This is the purifier" (*etat pavitram*) means it is that which purifies (*pāvanam*), i.e., it cleanses one from the evil that is the cause of the threefold suffering.
"Supreme" (*agryam*) means the foremost among all purifiers. "The sage" (*muniḥ*) refers to Kapila.
Out of compassion for Āsuri, he gave it to him; Āsuri, in turn, gave it to Pañcaśikha, and by him the Tantra was made manifold. || 70 ||
This has been handed down through a succession of disciples and composed in Āryā verses by Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
Having correctly understood the established tenet in brief by means of noble intelligence, || 71 ||
(277) The lineage of teachers and disciples of Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
(278) The status of the *Saptatikārikā* as a treatise (*śāstra*).
Regarding the word “śiṣya”: one who has gone far away from the [lower] principles (tattvas) is an Ārya; he whose intellect is that of an Ārya is this very person called “Āryamati. || 71 ||

And this is a *śāstra* (treatise), because it indicates the meaning of the entire *śāstra*, and not merely a *prakaraṇa* (section); thus he says: "The meanings which are in the Seventy [Verses] are indeed the meanings of the entire *Ṣaṣṭitantra*."
They are devoid of narratives and also free from the arguments of opponents. || 72 ||
"In the seventy" [is said]. And likewise, the Rājavārtika states:
The existence of the Pradhāna, its unity, its purposefulness, its distinctness, its subservience to another, as well as its multiplicity, disjunction, and conjunction.
Conclusion of the treatise:
Subsistence through remnants and non-agency are recorded as the fundamental topics;
likewise, the fivefold error and the nine contentments have been declared.
"The incapacity of the instruments is considered to be of twenty-eight kinds;
thus, there are sixty categories [of defects] along with the eight perfections."

Thus, since this has been stated as the "sixty categories" (*ṣaṣṭipadārthī*) through the exposition of the entire meaning of the treatise, it is established that this is not merely a section (*prakaraṇa*), but indeed the treatise (*śāstra*) itself. Oneness, purposefulness, and being for the sake of another are stated with reference to *pradhāna*.
Otherness, lack of agency, and multiplicity are stated with reference to *puruṣa*. Existence, disjunction, and conjunction—[are stated with reference to both].
Both [of these] are referred to by the term "functioning" (vṛtti); "subsistence" (sthiti) refers to both the gross and the subtle. || 72 ||
May the *Tattvakaumudī*, the work of the venerable Vācaspati Miśra, which always awakens the minds of the virtuous like white water-lilies, endure.
